questions.question: What belongs in an HTTP controller integration test?
questions.answer: Exercise routing, conversion/validation, serialization, status/error schema and applicable security/filter behavior through the actual HTTP/MVC boundary, with controlled external dependencies.

questions.question: How do you test 400, 401, 403, 404 and 409 responses?
questions.answer: Create distinct malformed, unauthenticated, unauthorized, missing and conflicting-resource fixtures; assert status, safe error body and relevant side-effect absence, not only an exception.

questions.question: What is consumer-driven contract testing?
questions.answer: Consumers publish the interactions/schema they rely on, and providers verify those contracts before release. Versioning/publication and real provider verification are essential.

questions.question: How does contract testing differ from end-to-end testing?
questions.answer: Contract tests check a service boundary's compatibility in controlled conditions; end-to-end tests exercise a broader deployed workflow and its actual integration behavior.

questions.question: How do you verify API backward compatibility?
questions.answer: Run representative supported old requests/payload readers against the new contract, checking requiredness, formats, enums, unknown fields, authentication and semantic behavior.

questions.question: How do you test idempotency using repeated POST requests?
questions.answer: Repeat and concurrently race the same scoped key/body; assert one durable business effect and documented replay/pending response. Test a changed body under the same key separately.

questions.question: How should you test malformed JSON and unknown fields?
questions.answer: Specify reject/ignore/default policy, then exercise actual converters/parsers for malformed syntax, wrong types and unknown fields/enums. Unknown accepted fields must not bypass invariants.

questions.question: What is the difference between MockMvc and WebTestClient?
questions.answer: MockMvc targets servlet MVC without requiring a live server; WebTestClient is a reactive-style HTTP testing client that can bind to supported servers/framework test adapters.

questions.question: How do you test error response bodies consistently?
questions.answer: Assert a shared schema and safe code/correlation/field details for each error category; exclude stack traces, secrets and incidental internal exception names.

questions.question: How do you exercise a third-party service failure without calling the real provider?
questions.answer: Use an HTTP stub/fake at the provider-client boundary to simulate rejection, malformed data, timeout and connection failure without real chargeable side effects.

questions.question: How do you test content-type negotiation?
questions.answer: Vary Content-Type and Accept, asserting successful chosen representation and documented 406/415/error behavior; include mismatched payload/type cases.

questions.question: When should WireMock simulate a downstream HTTP service?
questions.answer: When the HTTP protocol/client mapping itself needs testing: real request shape, headers, retry timing and classified failures against a controlled stub server.

questions.question: How do you verify a stable error schema?
questions.answer: Validate error responses against a versioned schema/contract and meaningful field assertions; prevent accidental sensitive details and unsupported enum/status changes.

questions.question: What is a snapshot test, and when can it be brittle?
questions.answer: It compares captured output with a stored expected representation. It becomes brittle when unordered fields, timestamps or irrelevant formatting dominate instead of stable semantics.

questions.question: A provider changes its response schema and breaks a consumer. How would contract tests catch it before deployment?
questions.answer: Publish versioned consumer expectations and have the actual provider implementation verify them before release. Include old/new schemas, null/enum/required-field behavior and error cases. A permissive stub that was never provider-verified merely confirms the consumer agrees with its own assumption.

questions.question: A POST endpoint creates two records on replay. What HTTP integration test would reveal it?
questions.answer: Race two identical POSTs with one tenant/key through independent requests, then verify one durable row/posting and the defined replay/pending result. Repeat after a simulated response-loss/crash boundary and test mismatched payload reuse; a sequential same-JVM test alone misses the cross-pod race.

questions.question: A security filter fails before MVC exception handling. What test would verify the actual public status?
questions.answer: Run the full SecurityFilterChain with anonymous, invalid-token and insufficient-permission fixtures and assert actual status/challenge/safe error shape. Standalone controller/advice tests cannot prove how an exception thrown before DispatcherServlet is rendered publicly.

questions.question: Can a balanced interval tree improve repeated online overlap queries after the one-off merge? Explain the workload difference.
questions.answer: Yes for repeated dynamic overlap lookup/update workloads. A one-off sorted merge needs only O(n log n) plus a scan; an interval tree adds indexing/maintenance complexity for different queries.

questions.question: During a cold implementation, state why no future interval can overlap a finalized output interval.
questions.answer: After sorting by start, a next interval starting beyond currentEnd cannot overlap the finalized span, and every later start is at least that large.

questions.question: If original interval IDs must be retained for audit, what metadata should accompany each merged span?
questions.answer: Carry provenance such as original interval IDs/source references alongside the union, with a defined many-to-one mapping and memory/audit policy.

questions.question: Explain how merging closed intervals differs from coalescing adjacent integer ranges such as [1,2] and [3,4].
questions.answer: Closed intervals must overlap to merge under an overlap-only rule; integer-adjacent [1,2] and [3,4] have no shared point but may be coalesced under a separate discrete-adjacency contract.

questions.question: When the same input list is reused by another caller, how could in-place sorting introduce an unexpected side effect?
questions.answer: Another caller observes reordered input even if endpoint arrays are copied. Copy the outer collection before sorting when the API promises read-only ownership.

questions.question: During the second session, implement the sweep without reference code and state exactly when a span is appended to the output.
questions.answer: Append/finalize the active span only when the next start cannot overlap it, then start a new active span; append the final active span after traversal.

questions.question: What is throughput versus response time?
questions.answer: Throughput is completed operations per unit time; response time is elapsed request duration including defined queue/network phases. One can improve while the other worsens.

questions.question: What do p50, p95 and p99 latency mean?
questions.answer: They are percentile boundaries of an explicitly defined latency population. Report successes, errors/timeouts and the measurement window so percentiles are not misleadingly selective.

questions.question: What is the difference between load, stress and soak tests?
questions.answer: Load tests expected demand; stress finds failure/saturation beyond it; soak tests prolonged behavior such as leaks, drift and resource exhaustion.

questions.question: How can a closed-loop load generator hide overload?
questions.answer: A response-paced generator omits requests that would have arrived while it was stalled, understating overload delay relative to a fixed arrival process.

questions.question: How would an open-loop load test expose latency omitted by a response-paced generator, and what arrival-rate evidence must be retained?
questions.answer: Schedule arrivals independently of responses and record intended versus actual send times, dropped/late arrivals and all outcomes. A saturated generator can still invalidate the offered-load claim.

questions.question: Why is average latency misleading under tail spikes?
questions.answer: A small slow/error fraction can harm users while the mean improves. Inspect tails and failure rates, particularly under concurrency and retries.

questions.question: How do you identify the saturation point of a service?
questions.answer: Increase offered load and find where queues/latency/errors grow while useful completed throughput stops increasing; keep data and correctness/SLO constraints explicit.

questions.question: How do you separate application bottlenecks from load-generator bottlenecks?
questions.answer: Measure generator CPU/network, send lateness and connection limits separately from server resources; distribute/scale the generator only while preserving accurate arrival accounting.

questions.question: Which metrics reveal database connection pool contention?
questions.answer: Active are borrowed, idle are available, pending are waiting borrowers; sampled values vary concurrently and need correlation with duration/throughput. Add acquisition duration/timeouts, borrower ages and actual database waits.

questions.question: How do you decide whether a change improved capacity without increasing errors?
questions.answer: Compare equal workload and SLO with useful completions, latency distribution, errors/timeouts/rejections and resource cost. Faster successful responses alone can hide discarded work.

questions.question: How do you calculate requests per second from completed requests?
questions.answer: Divide relevant completed requests by the actual elapsed measurement interval; label whether failures, warmup and partial requests are included.

questions.question: What is the meaning of Little's Law in service capacity?
questions.answer: For a stable system, mean in-flight population L equals arrival/completion rate lambda times mean time W, using consistent boundaries. Unbounded queues violate steady-state assumptions.

questions.question: Why can more threads decrease throughput?
questions.answer: Oversubscription adds context switching, cache/coherence traffic, contention and downstream overload. Additional waiting threads do not add CPU or database capacity.

questions.question: How do you choose a representative test data distribution?
questions.answer: Match sizes, skew/hot keys, read/write mix, tenant distribution, errors and data age/volume to the business workload, including representative worst-supported cases.

questions.question: A new release doubles p99 latency while average improves. What would you tell the release owner?
questions.answer: Report that the average gain does not satisfy the tail SLO and show p95/p99, timeout/rejection/error rates at equivalent offered load. Identify the changed path/queueing cause before release; shipping requires an explicit accepted trade-off, not a selective average-only success claim.

questions.question: A load test saturates the client generator before the server. How do you identify invalid measurements?
questions.answer: Check actual versus scheduled sends, generator CPU/network/connection queues and late/dropped arrivals. Those data cannot establish server capacity if the client never offered the claimed load. Increase generator capability and rerun with complete arrival/outcome accounting.

questions.question: An API is fast in staging with small data but slow in production. What workload factors would you replicate?
questions.answer: Replicate data volume/skew, hot accounts, index/statistics state, concurrency, network/provider tails, cache hit distribution and production limits. Compare plans and queue/resource behavior rather than only copying the same endpoint code into a smaller environment.

questions.question: What state should remain unchanged after a failed dequeue on an empty ring?
questions.answer: Storage, head, tail and size remain unchanged. Returning a failure must not consume a phantom element or move the logical front.

questions.question: Implement the size-based ring representation with an int[] and constant-time operations.
questions.answer: Use head plus size to derive next insertion/rear, reject full/empty operations before mutation and wrap valid indices; the appendix contains the complete class.

questions.question: How do you test repeated wraparound rather than just the first pass through the array?
questions.answer: Generate several fill/drain/interleaved cycles with monotonically labeled values and compare each result against a capacity-limited reference ArrayDeque.

questions.question: If capacity zero is allowed, how must you avoid modulo by zero?
questions.answer: Reject/no-op operations before calculating any modulo when capacity==0, or disallow zero capacity at construction explicitly.

questions.question: Why should a general ring buffer clear removed object references even though an int[] version need not?
questions.answer: Object arrays otherwise retain references to removed values until overwritten, extending their lifetime. Primitive array slots do not retain heap objects.

questions.question: What difference does a reserved-slot representation make to allocated array length versus advertised capacity?
questions.answer: A reserved-slot design normally allocates advertisedCapacity+1 slots so head==tail unambiguously means empty while the next tail position detects full.

questions.question: Why does mocking a repository hide database constraint behavior?
questions.answer: Run conflicting writes through real persistence/commit boundaries and assert specific constraint/outcome behavior from independent reads; a mocked repository cannot enforce SQL rules.

questions.question: How do you reproduce concurrency bugs without sleep?
questions.answer: Gate the relevant conflicting read/update phases, use independent worker state and await all outcomes, then assert the shared invariant under that forced interleaving.

questions.question: What causes contract tests to fail after response schema changes?
questions.answer: Actual requiredness/type/enum/error semantics no longer match published expectations; provider verification must run against real implementation, not only old stubs.

questions.question: Why does p99 latency matter more than average in an overloaded API?
questions.answer: It exposes the slow minority affected by queueing, retries and contention; report error/timeouts too rather than treating one percentile as the entire service contract.

questions.question: When is Testcontainers preferable to H2?
questions.answer: It starts a real database/service implementation in a controlled container, exercising its dialect, constraints and transaction behavior instead of an in-memory substitute's approximations.

questions.question: How do you test an idempotent endpoint with concurrent callers?
questions.answer: Use separate concurrent request/transaction paths sharing a stable key, force the reservation race and assert one authoritative effect plus correct replay/conflict semantics.

questions.question: What evidence proves a race was fixed?
questions.answer: A correct synchronization/atomicity argument, a deterministic regression for the old bad schedule and invariant-based stress/property evidence together; no finite clean run proves every possible schedule.

questions.question: Why should unit tests not assert incidental private-method calls?
questions.answer: Private calls are refactorable structure. Assert public results and required collaborator effects so harmless internal restructuring does not break meaningful tests.

questions.question: How do test doubles differ from real integrations?
questions.answer: Fakes/stubs approximate selected behaviors; real integrations execute actual lifecycle, serialization, protocol and database/broker constraints. Use each at the boundary it can genuinely validate.

questions.question: What should a failed negative API test assert about response structure?
questions.answer: Assert status plus the safe versioned error schema, code/field context and side-effect absence, excluding stack traces, credentials and internal implementation leakage.

questions.question: A mocked DAO hides a duplicate-key failure. What real database integration test is missing?
questions.answer: Race real inserts against the actual unique business constraint on the supported database family, ending each transaction and verifying one committed winner plus the losing replay/conflict behavior. A mocked DAO cannot generate the authoritative constraint/interleaving semantics being claimed.

questions.question: A concurrency test is flaky because it uses Thread.sleep. How would latches help?
questions.answer: Replace sleep with gates for started, conflicting-phase and completed events, each with bounded await and exception reporting. Force the specific old failure, then run the fix through the same schedule. A start latch without completion or phase coordination is still incomplete evidence.

questions.question: A response contract change breaks consumers at rollout. What predeployment validation should catch it?
questions.answer: Publish versioned consumer expectations and have the actual provider implementation verify them before release. Include old/new schemas, null/enum/required-field behavior and error cases. A permissive stub that was never provider-verified merely confirms the consumer agrees with its own assumption.

questions.question: How would a test compare random operations against a simple stack plus a linear minimum scan?
questions.answer: Generate valid/invalid pushes,pops,top/min calls, compare with a simple list stack and linear min oracle, and preserve failing random seeds/operation histories.

questions.question: When memory is tight, which value distributions let a compressed minima stack save space, and when does its worst case remain linear?
questions.answer: Few new minima permit compressed records/counts; strictly decreasing values create a new minimum every push, so worst-case extra storage remains O(n).

questions.question: If the contract adds getMax, what additional state can be maintained symmetrically?
questions.answer: Maintain maximum-so-far with each prefix or a duplicate-aware maxima stack alongside the minima representation; update all associated state atomically if concurrent.

questions.question: What shared-state race appears when push and getMin access two separate stacks concurrently?
questions.answer: A reader can observe values and minima between their separate updates, returning a minimum inconsistent with the visible stack. Coordinate the composite operation.

questions.question: A Mockito test verifies an internal helper invocation but misses an incorrect returned amount. Which observable assertion should replace it?
questions.answer: Assert the returned exact amount/currency and required durable/collaborator effects, including rounding and rejection cases, instead of only verifying an incidental helper ran.

questions.question: A transaction test rolls back automatically and never reads through a new connection. Which production commit behavior remains unverified?
questions.answer: It has not proved the application's real boundary commits successfully or rolls back failures; in-context values can pass without durable external verification.

questions.question: A load generator waits for each response before sending the next request. Which overload latency can its schedule hide?
questions.answer: A response-paced generator omits requests that would have arrived while it was stalled, understating overload delay relative to a fixed arrival process.

questions.question: A controller test builds a standalone controller and bypasses security. What separate full-chain test is needed?
questions.answer: Add a context/full-chain HTTP test exercising actual authentication, authorization, CSRF/CORS as intended and the public error response before MVC.

questions.question: A contract stub accepts every enum value but production rejects unknown ones. Which provider verification step is missing?
questions.answer: The stub/contract was not verified against the real provider's enum acceptance/forward-compatibility behavior. Include concrete unknown-value negative/compatibility cases.

questions.question: A race test coordinates starts with a latch yet asserts before both workers finish. Which completion barrier is absent?
questions.answer: A completion latch, joined Futures or tracked final stages with bounded waits and exception observation is missing.

questions.question: An integration test reuses mutable seed data across cases. How can execution order mask a failed constraint?
questions.answer: One case can prepopulate/correct state another depends on, hiding isolation/constraint errors. Use deterministic independent fixtures and explicit cleanup.

questions.question: A client aborts at a deadline, but the server continues charging. Which timeout test must assert side effects as well as the response?
questions.answer: Force provider acceptance then local/client timeout, verify one durable effect and reconciliation/replay behavior. A timeout response does not mean the bank/DB action was cancelled.

questions.question: A load test reports p99 only for successes. How should timeouts, errors and rejections be reported alongside it?
questions.answer: Report latency population alongside offered/completed load and timeout/error/rejection counts/rates; censored or excluded outcomes must not disappear from the SLO.

questions.question: A database fixture starts with an empty schema only. Which migration test needs a previous-release data snapshot?
questions.answer: Start from the previous-release schema plus representative existing data, then migrate and run compatibility/content assertions, including restart/partial progress.

questions.question: A load test shows good averages but poor tail latency. How would you report failure?
questions.answer: Report the full latency distribution, SLO threshold, affected fraction and errors/timeouts at the stated offered load. Explain that good averages do not compensate for a breached user-facing tail objective, and identify whether queueing, a hot cohort or downstream tails dominate.

questions.question: A controller integration test bypasses security filters. How would you ensure full chain coverage?
questions.answer: Run the full SecurityFilterChain with anonymous, invalid-token and insufficient-permission fixtures and assert actual status/challenge/safe error shape. Standalone controller/advice tests cannot prove how an exception thrown before DispatcherServlet is rendered publicly.

questions.question: An external API retry is tested against the actual provider and incurs charges. What test double boundary is appropriate?
questions.answer: Stub the external provider at the real HTTP client boundary and verify request identity, timeout/retry and malformed-response handling there. Keep live provider tests separately controlled under its test/sandbox contract; a unit/integration retry test must not create real customer charges.

questions.question: How could a negative remainder in Java appear when computing rear with tail-1?
questions.answer: Java remainder can stay negative: (0-1)%capacity is -1. Add capacity before modulo or use a correct floorMod formulation.

questions.question: Which operation sequence exposes an off-by-one full check when size equals capacity?
questions.answer: Fill exactly capacity slots, attempt one more enqueue and assert rejection with unchanged state; then dequeue one and verify exactly one new insertion succeeds.

questions.question: Compare the ring queue's fixed memory with the earlier two-stack queue under unbounded growth.
questions.answer: A fixed ring bounds storage and rejects/waits at capacity; an unbounded two-stack queue grows with demand and supplies no automatic admission limit.

questions.question: If enqueue and dequeue run on separate threads, which publication and atomicity questions appear beyond index arithmetic?
questions.answer: Publishing element contents and coherent head/size/tail updates requires a valid happens-before/linearization protocol. Separate atomic indices do not by themselves prove safe FIFO behavior.

days.focus: Recall two weak distributed-systems/LLD/testing topics; prove one crash-boundary invariant with a small trace or test.

questions.question: What does Kafka guarantee when a consumer crashes after committing to SQL?
questions.answer: Kafka may replay from the earlier committed group position; it does not undo the SQL commit. Use a stable business/event identity with atomic dedupe plus business changes, supported external idempotency and a bounded recovery/reconciliation contract.

questions.question: Refill time advances correctly but two callers read one remaining token; which combined state update must be atomic?
questions.answer: Protect refill timestamp, token balance and consumption as one state transition with a lock or correct atomic aggregate. An atomic token counter alone is insufficient.

questions.question: How do you test a cache's list-map consistency under concurrent eviction?
questions.answer: Gate get/update/evict conflicts and assert map/list bijection, no duplicate live nodes, neighbor symmetry and correct capacity/recency under the stated linearization policy.

questions.question: What can a contract test prove that Mockito cannot?
questions.answer: Provider-verified contracts check actual boundary compatibility; mocks merely implement local programmed expectations and cannot establish the remote implementation agrees.

questions.question: Why can a saga compensation fail after the original step succeeded?
questions.answer: A compensation is another independently failing business operation, not a guaranteed rollback. Give it a stable compensation ID, durable state/version checks and safe retry rules; distinguish definite failure from unknown external outcome.

questions.question: How does Redis TTL interact with stale read windows?
questions.answer: TTL bounds cache validity only under its checking/fill protocol. Old in-flight reads or lost invalidation can repopulate stale state after expiry/commit.

questions.question: What makes an outbox relay at-least-once rather than exactly-once?
questions.answer: No atomic commit spans broker publish acknowledgement and the relay's SQL sent marker in the ordinary pattern; a crash can occur between them.

questions.question: How can a payment ledger invariant be tested with two threads?
questions.answer: Gate conflicting operations on independent authoritative transactions, assert journal balance/uniqueness and allowed final states, then verify through a fresh read.

questions.question: What does an overloaded consumer group look like?
questions.answer: Growing per-partition lag/oldest age, processing slower than arrivals, repeated timeouts/rebalances and saturated dependency/worker queues; idle members can still coexist with one hot partition.

questions.question: Why does a thread-safe map not automatically make an LRU cache thread-safe?
questions.answer: Use one invariant-wide lock initially, or a carefully defined segmented/ownership policy that protects map membership and linked-list updates together.

questions.question: When is a short-lived dependency outage not a reason to fail a workflow permanently?
questions.answer: When durable retry/recovery can safely resume within the business's allowed pending horizon. Expose pending rather than permanently failing an accepted operation prematurely.

questions.question: Why does a DLQ need a replay procedure?
questions.answer: Without scoped ownership, compatibility/idempotency checks and an audit trail, quarantined work remains unresolved or is replayed unsafely as duplicate effects.

questions.question: What kind of test detects a provider's backward-incompatible field change?
questions.answer: Run representative supported old requests/payload readers against the new contract, checking requiredness, formats, enums, unknown fields, authentication and semantic behavior. Include actual consumer-provider verification, not only a permissive mock.

questions.question: How do you define a measurable correctness guarantee for a distributed API?
questions.answer: State a testable invariant and failure boundary, such as one balanced posting per tenant/operation ID despite retries, with durability, ordering and recovery horizons explicit.

questions.question: A consumer catches all exceptions and commits offsets. How can this cause irreversible data loss?
questions.answer: The consumer records progress past a failed business action, so restart begins after work that never committed. Stop/rollback or quarantine durably according to the ordering policy, then advance only safe progress. finally is not the correct unconditional acknowledgement rule.

questions.question: A token bucket accepts too many requests under concurrent use. What race test should fail?
questions.answer: Place two callers at one-token availability before consumption and assert exactly one succeeds. Also race refill and consume under the fake clock, checking 0<=tokens<=capacity and accepted quota. Both tests must fail against the broken separated-check/decrement implementation.

questions.question: A mock-only test claims transaction safety. What real DB behavior remains unverified?
questions.answer: Mocks do not execute unique/version constraints, rollback/commit boundaries, isolation, deadlocks or flush-time database errors. Use independent real connections/contexts and fresh post-completion assertions for the specific claimed invariant.

questions.question: Why does reaching a terminal course not prove that the rest of the prerequisite graph is acyclic?
questions.answer: A terminal node proves only that one path ends. Other components or branches can still contain a directed cycle.

questions.question: How can an independent cycle coexist with a large acyclic component that Kahn's algorithm processes successfully?
questions.answer: An acyclic component drains normally while cycle members never reach zero indegree; compare processed count with every course, including isolated nodes.

questions.question: If new prerequisite edges are added over time, what limitation does recomputing a full topological order have?
questions.answer: Recomputing costs O(V+E) per change and may be too expensive for high-rate online updates. Incremental maintenance introduces a different algorithm/complexity trade-off.

questions.question: What input validation prevents a course index outside 0..numCourses-1 from corrupting graph construction?
questions.answer: Require every course and prerequisite endpoint to lie in [0,numCourses), validating edge shape and the documented duplicate policy before indexing arrays.

questions.question: How would you derive time and space separately in vertices V and prerequisite edges E?
questions.answer: Each vertex enters the ready queue at most once and each edge decrements once: O(V+E) time; adjacency, indegrees and frontier use O(V+E) space.

questions.question: Why can a recursion color accidentally left active after returning create false cycle reports?
questions.answer: Later cross edges see a completed node falsely marked active and report a nonexistent back-edge cycle. Mark completed on every normal DFS return.

questions.question: Rebuild a minimal outbox schema: which uniqueness and sent-state fields are useful?
questions.answer: Store immutable event_id, aggregate_id/version, payload/schema version, created/available time and delivery/claim/attempt state; choose indexes/uniqueness from the relay/recovery contract.

questions.question: Implement an idempotent consumer with one SQL transaction and an event ID.
questions.answer: Insert the unique processed-event key and apply the business change in the same transaction; on a recognized duplicate replay the stored result after correct transaction cleanup.

questions.question: Write a fake-clock test that proves token refill after elapsed monotonic time.
questions.answer: Inject a clock, advance deterministic increments and test exact refill/capacity boundaries, concurrent last-token use and no real sleeps.

questions.question: Implement LRU eviction and show behavior when an existing key is updated.
questions.answer: The least-recently accessed real node, not necessarily the oldest inserted one.

questions.question: Build a Spring integration test that asserts rollback on a duplicate transaction.
questions.answer: Invoke the real transaction proxy against a database constraint, force a duplicate failure and verify all intended changes rolled back through a fresh connection.

questions.question: Write a saga state transition table with one compensation path.
questions.answer: Persist states such as RESERVED->PAYMENT_PENDING->COMPLETED, or PAYMENT_FAILED->RELEASE_PENDING->RELEASED, with guarded transitions and explicit unknown/manual-review outcomes.

questions.question: Implement Redis cache-aside with explicit invalidation after commit.
questions.answer: Load on miss, publish only compatible committed versions, and use an after-commit durable invalidation/retry path where lost notifications matter. Test stale in-flight fills.

questions.question: Write a contract test for a provider's changed JSON response.
questions.answer: Send actual old/new response fixtures through the consumer parser and verify them against the provider contract, including unknown enum/required-field/error behavior.

questions.question: Construct a Kafka replay test after DB success but before offset commit.
questions.answer: Within one database transaction, attempt a unique stable event/business identity and apply the invoice change only for the winner. On replay, recognize the committed outcome and advance safely without another invoice. Verify crash-before/after-commit points and retention beyond permitted replay time.

questions.question: Implement a ledger debit and credit as one atomic unit.
questions.answer: Write the full balanced journal transaction in one local database transaction with validation/constraints and an explicit committed state. Do not independently commit its two sides.

questions.question: Show a rate-limit algorithm that works across two competing threads.
questions.answer: Treat elapsed-time refill, availability check and decrement as one critical section/atomic script. Align two callers at a one-token boundary and assert exactly one acceptance. Separately test that a refill racing with consumption neither loses tokens nor exceeds capacity.

questions.question: Build a negative test for a duplicate idempotency key with mismatched body.
questions.answer: Race/replay one tenant/key with two different normalized payload fingerprints and assert conflict with the original outcome unchanged and no second business effect.

questions.question: Implement a bounded queue and demonstrate capacity exhaustion.
questions.answer: Use a fixed-capacity BlockingQueue/ring with documented rejection/wait policy and prove the first over-capacity insertion does not silently lose accepted work.

questions.question: Write a load test with explicit p95 and p99 assertions.
questions.answer: Define arrival/data mix and p95/p99 plus error/rejection SLOs, measure all outcomes and generator capability, and fail the test on the actual relevant objective.

questions.question: Your outbox relay publishes a duplicate event after crash. What should the payment consumer do?
questions.answer: Within one database transaction, attempt a unique stable event/business identity and apply the invoice change only for the winner. On replay, recognize the committed outcome and advance safely without another invoice. Verify crash-before/after-commit points and retention beyond permitted replay time.

questions.question: Your LRU cache changes eviction order under interleaving. What synchronization proof is missing?
questions.answer: A successful get must atomically confirm membership and move that exact live node to MRU relative to eviction. Reproduce get-versus-evict interleavings and assert map/list bijection, neighbor symmetry and live-node count. Independently thread-safe map calls cannot protect this composite state.

questions.question: A saga loses state after restart. What durable state transition model restores it?
questions.answer: Persist each allowed state/version transition and outbound intent atomically in local storage, preserving original step IDs across restarts. On recovery, reconcile uncertain external steps and claim the next allowed transition, rather than rebuilding a process-local saga from a guessed latest callback.

questions.question: If a minimum one-house selection is mandatory, which empty-choice assumption changes?
questions.answer: Returning zero for all-negative/empty-choice paths is no longer always valid. Track whether any house was selected and reject empty input or choose the best required single selection.

questions.question: How would integer overflow alter a maximum-sum comparison even when the structural DP is correct?
questions.answer: Wrapped sums can reverse a max comparison and choose the wrong path. Use long/BigInteger or checked bounds before arithmetic, not after the value has overflowed.

questions.question: What property says appending a zero-value house cannot reduce the optimal total?
questions.answer: Ignoring the appended zero is always an available old solution, so the optimal value cannot decrease when no selection is required.

questions.question: How would doubling every nonnegative house value affect the optimal value and chosen-set ties?
questions.answer: The optimum value doubles; relative ordering of valid subset sums and ties remains unchanged under exact nonnegative scaling without overflow.

questions.question: Why is sorting house values invalid even if it helps a greedy selection appear simpler?
questions.answer: Sorting changes which positions are adjacent, destroying the constraint. The original street order is part of the problem, not an incidental representation.

questions.question: Construct two prefixes with the same best total but different best totals excluding the last house; why are two states needed?
questions.answer: Prefixes [5] and [5,0] both have best 5 but two-back/excluding-last values 0 and 5; appending the same value can therefore need different take results.

questions.question: A consumer reprocesses a refund after rebalance and doubles the payout. What idempotency boundary failed?
questions.answer: Durable dedupe must be atomic with refund intent/posting and stable provider operation identity. Deduplicate at the durable business-effect boundary, atomically with local refund intent/state and the original event ID. Reuse a stable provider refund operation reference and reconcile unknown external outcomes. Committing an offset or using a local Set cannot undo an already sent duplicate refund.

questions.question: A cache serves an old ledger balance after a successful commit. How would you fix ordering?
questions.answer: Publish/invalidate after commit and reject stale fill versions/generations. A later old read must not overwrite the canonical committed balance in cache.

questions.question: A saga state says completed though one provider timed out. How would you reconcile uncertain outcome?
questions.answer: Retain unknown/pending status, query the original provider reference and finalize through a guarded transition; a timeout alone does not justify completed.

questions.question: A token-bucket test flakes around exact refill times. How would you remove wall-clock assumptions?
questions.answer: Inject a clock, advance deterministic increments and test exact refill/capacity boundaries, concurrent last-token use and no real sleeps.

questions.question: An LRU cache corrupts pointers under concurrent operations. Which invariant was not synchronized?
questions.answer: The map-to-unique-live-node bijection and linked-neighbor consistency must be protected together across get/put/evict operations.

questions.question: An outbox relay deletes a row before publication acknowledgement and loses an event. What recovery property was lost?
questions.answer: The durable intent was destroyed before safe publication/recovery evidence existed. Retain retryable rows until the chosen acknowledgement/retention policy is satisfied.

questions.question: A test mocks a database and misses a uniqueness collision. What integration scenario is required?
questions.answer: Race real equal business-key inserts on independent transactions, observe the actual unique violation/replay result and verify one committed effect.

questions.question: A Redis lease expires during a long-running task. Why might a stale owner still write?
questions.answer: Lease expiry does not halt execution. Lease expiry does not stop a paused old process. Require an authoritative monotonically increasing fencing/version token checked on writes, or a different safe idempotent operation protocol. A Redis lock's unique release value prevents deleting another lease, but is not itself downstream fencing.

questions.question: A Kafka message is routed to the wrong key partition and arrives out of order. What changes preserve per-key order?
questions.answer: Choose a stable aggregate key and enforce sequence/version checks, coordinating topology/async processing where broker partition order alone no longer suffices.

questions.question: An API returns success before an async queue write is durable. What guarantee did it incorrectly claim?
questions.answer: It claimed durable acceptance without persisting a recoverable obligation. A process crash can lose the queued operation after the client received success.

questions.question: A circuit breaker opens too late while the worker pool is already saturated. What complementary controls are needed?
questions.answer: Add earlier admission/in-flight/queue limits and actual transport deadlines; a health window can react only after resources are already being consumed.

questions.question: A provider contract changes an enum value and consumers crash. What compatibility policy helps?
questions.answer: Versioned tolerant/explicit-rejection parsing and provider/consumer compatibility tests, including unknown enum values. Never silently reinterpret a new financial state as success.

questions.question: A consumer maps unknown event enum values to null; which compatibility test should force an explicit forward-compatibility decision?
questions.answer: Pass a realistic unknown enum through the actual parser and business logic, asserting the chosen safe forward-compatible fallback or explicit rejection instead of accidental null behavior.

questions.question: A batch event processor crashes on a poison message. How would you keep other partitions progressing?
questions.answer: Isolate errors/progress per partition with bounded classified retries/quarantine, while committing only safe contiguous offsets and preserving affected aggregate ordering/recovery rules.

questions.question: An outage produces stale Redis balances and duplicate Kafka events simultaneously. Where is the source of truth?
questions.answer: The authoritative durable ledger/operation store, protected by unique IDs and transaction/state invariants, remains the source of truth. Treat Redis as a performance copy and Kafka as replayable transport. Reconcile unknown external effects with stable references before repairing projections/caches.

questions.question: A DLQ grows for days but dashboards show normal success. Which SLO is misleading?
questions.answer: Immediate handler/broker success is hiding unresolved business work. Track end-to-end completion age, DLQ age/backlog and replay outcome against the delivery/recovery SLO. Quarantining an event is not the same as completing its financial obligation.

questions.question: A monitoring rollout labels every payment ID and exhausts series capacity. What evidence should move to logs/traces, and which aggregate labels remain?
questions.answer: Move per-payment IDs and detailed evidence into controlled logs/traces; retain bounded endpoint, error category, service, region and similar aggregate dimensions. Preserve correlation links without creating a time series per customer/transaction.

questions.question: Implement detach and attachMostRecent helpers; which neighbor pointers must each update?
questions.answer: detach rewires node.prev.next and node.next.prev; attachMRU links node between head and its former first real neighbor, updating all four neighboring references.

questions.question: How should a cache get distinguish a missing key from a stored value of -1 in a generalized API?
questions.answer: Use an explicit presence result/Optional-like value or a documented exception. -1 cannot be both an ordinary cached value and an unambiguous miss.

questions.question: Does a get miss change recency of any existing key? Explain the expected state.
questions.answer: No under the standard LRU contract: missing keys have no entry to promote, and other entries' relative order stays unchanged.

questions.question: If put replaces the current least-recent key, should that key become most recent?
questions.answer: Yes. An update is an access under the usual LRU definition, so replace the value and move that same node to MRU.

questions.question: How would LinkedHashMap accessOrder=true implement the same policy, and what eviction hook is needed?
questions.answer: Enable accessOrder and override removeEldestEntry to enforce capacity for a simple implementation. Synchronize composite operations if concurrency is part of the contract.

questions.question: What test detects a self-loop after moving an already most-recent node?
questions.answer: Perform repeated get/put on the current MRU and traverse both directions with identity/cycle checks; every real node must appear once with consistent neighbors.

days.focus: Answer three distributed-system prompts, then fix one previously failed implementation or test.

questions.question: Implement one SQL idempotency record insert with a unique event ID.
questions.answer: INSERT INTO processed_event(consumer_id,event_id) VALUES(:consumer,:event); enforce the matching UNIQUE key and include the business effect in that same transaction.

questions.question: Write code that compares stale cache data with the canonical database value.
questions.answer: Read/cache the version with the value and compare to an authorized authoritative query; reject stale generations and instrument discrepancy age without logging sensitive ledger payloads.

questions.question: Design a concurrency test for simultaneous balance withdrawals.
questions.answer: Instrument a test seam between counter read and write. Use two barriers so both threads read the old value before either writes, then assert the lost result. This proves the faulty interleaving instead of depending on sleep or repeated lucky stress runs. Apply the forced schedule to independent authoritative transactions and assert balance/journal invariants, not only a test counter.

questions.question: Trace Kafka offset and DB commit in all crash-order permutations.
questions.answer: DB-before-offset may replay and needs dedupe; offset-before-DB may lose work; crash-before-both retries cleanly. External success/unknown outcomes add an independent recovery branch.

questions.question: Build an LRU cache with TTL using an injectable clock.
questions.answer: Use the structural lock protocol plus injected monotonic expiry checks; tests cover exact expiry, miss/reload generations and capacity eviction independently.

questions.question: Write a token bucket that rejects the sixth request when capacity is five.
questions.answer: With a fixed fake time and initially five tokens, atomically consume five, reject the sixth without changing state, then advance enough time and verify bounded refill.

questions.question: Implement an outbox relay loop with bounded retries.
questions.answer: Claim a bounded ordered batch durably, publish original event IDs with deadlines, mark acknowledged work and recover abandoned claims; classify/quarantine exhausted poison events without deleting recoverable intent.

questions.question: Write a saga compensation command that can be invoked twice safely.
questions.answer: Give the compensation a unique original-step-derived ID, persist its guarded state and reuse the provider reference; a second invocation replays/reconciles the first outcome.

questions.question: Implement a contract test that rejects an unexpected provider field change.
questions.answer: Verify actual parser/consumer semantics against published provider fixtures/implementation, including required types/enums. Ignore only explicitly allowed additive changes, not every unknown value.

questions.question: Build a metric for DLQ growth with bounded labels.
questions.answer: Track DLQ count/oldest age and replay results by bounded service/topic/error category; keep event IDs in controlled logs/traces rather than metric labels.

questions.question: Write a test proving an HTTP timeout does not silently cancel a committed transaction.
questions.answer: Force commit before an artificial lost response/deadline, then read durable state and replay the same identity. Assert timeout does not imply the completed effect vanished.

questions.question: Your strategy registry has two beans claiming one provider code; how should startup validation report the collision?
questions.answer: Fail startup with the conflicting canonical provider code and safe bean identities. Do not arbitrarily keep first/last registration or defer the collision to a random request.

questions.question: Write a load test that distinguishes p50 from p99 regression.
questions.answer: Report both distributions plus errors under equal offered load/data; fail a p99 SLO regression even if p50/mean improves.

questions.question: Demonstrate a dead-letter replay that preserves event identity.
questions.answer: Select a bounded explicit DLQ range, revalidate schema/business state, republish the original logical event ID and record operator/reason/outcome without duplicating committed effects.

questions.question: Your deterministic race test can reproduce double charging. What actual production guard would you add?
questions.answer: Enforce stable operation uniqueness/payload identity and an atomic funds/state/journal transaction at the production authority, with provider idempotency/reconciliation for remote charges. Keep the deterministic failing schedule as a regression. A test harness lock is not a production guard across pods.

questions.question: An outbox replay is implemented by restarting everything. How would you make replay scoped and auditable?
questions.answer: Build a replay command scoped by stable IDs/time range, with dry-run/authorization where useful, preserved event identity, version/business validation and per-item audited outcomes. Bound rate and monitor recovery. Restarting everything gives poor control and can repeat already completed effects.

questions.question: A load test shows lower average latency but worse customer complaints. Which percentile metrics matter?
questions.answer: Compare p95/p99/p99.9 where justified, timeout/rejection/error rates, queue wait and slow cohort/dependency distributions at equivalent load. Lower average can mask a badly degraded minority or discarded work; tie the decision to the documented user-facing SLO.

questions.question: How would a caller-supplied result limit change the recursion's stopping rules?
questions.answer: Stop exploring once the requested number of immutable results is emitted, checking cancellation/limit at recursion boundaries. Define whether output order determines which subset is returned.

questions.question: What makes Generate Parentheses an output-sensitive problem rather than a linear-time string scan?
questions.answer: It must emit C_n sequences of length 2n, so work grows with output size, not just input n. Prefix pruning cannot eliminate required copying.

questions.question: If the requested output is only a count, how does the task differ from storing every generated String?
questions.answer: Compute the Catalan count or a counting DP without constructing every string, with a sufficient numeric type. The objective and memory/output lower bound change.

questions.question: How would you check each generated result with the earlier Valid Parentheses implementation?
questions.answer: Validate every generated string's nesting and length, then separately check uniqueness/completeness for small n. A valid-subset generator can still miss required outputs.

questions.question: Construct a test verifying that every output has exactly n opening and n closing symbols.
questions.answer: For every result assert length 2n, exactly n '(' and n ')', and all prefix balances nonnegative; compare known small-n output sets.

questions.question: Why can a single mutable result list reused between calls leak old generated strings?
questions.answer: A later invocation may retain prior n/results unless the result container is fresh or explicitly cleared under a safe ownership contract.

days.focus: Run a 25-minute distributed-system mock and use 30 minutes for one executable correction.

questions.question: How does at-least-once Kafka delivery change payment-system design?
questions.answer: Use a stable business/event identity with atomic dedupe plus business changes, supported external idempotency and a bounded recovery/reconciliation contract.

questions.question: What is the consistency boundary of a SQL transaction with an outbox?
questions.answer: Business state and publication intent are atomic only within their shared local database transaction. Broker/consumer/external effects still have later retry/consistency boundaries.

questions.question: Why should a distributed cache not own the ledger balance?
questions.answer: When its configured durability/failover/eviction cannot meet the business invariant, especially using a short-lived performance cache as the sole financial identity/balance authority.

questions.question: How do you prevent rate-limit bypass across multiple app pods?
questions.answer: Coordinate one atomic shared quota state or preallocated bounded regional/pod budgets with a stated overshoot/failure policy. Six independent 100-RPS counters permit roughly six times a global 100-RPS target. Choose availability versus exact global admission explicitly.

questions.question: What is the functional difference between compensation and rollback?
questions.answer: It is a new business action intended to offset an earlier committed effect, which may be imperfect, fail or be impossible. Database rollback undoes uncommitted local changes.

questions.question: Why can a successful mock API test conceal a broken contract?
questions.answer: The mock may encode outdated assumptions and never run the real provider parser/protocol. Verify published contracts against the provider implementation.

questions.question: What can a deterministic concurrency test establish that a stress test cannot?
questions.answer: It forces a known bad schedule and validates the repaired invariant there. Stress adds broader schedules but cannot guarantee hitting that specific rare interleaving.

questions.question: How would you explain LRU's O(1) property with concrete structures?
questions.answer: The map finds a node directly; its doubly linked pointers detach/reattach it without scanning. Hash lookup is expected O(1), pointer work O(1).

questions.question: What happens if an idempotency key expires while the original request retries?
questions.answer: If durable business identity also disappears, replay can execute again. Retention must cover all allowed retry/replay/unknown-outcome horizons independently of response-cache TTL.

questions.question: When should an outbox message be quarantined for manual repair?
questions.answer: When retries cannot fix its classified payload/state problem or safe processing needs operator evidence. Preserve identity, reason and audit/replay ownership instead of deleting it silently.

questions.question: Which system metrics reveal consumer underprovisioning?
questions.answer: Per-partition lag/age and processing rate, assignments, queue/DB waits, failed/retried batches and available downstream capacity; more members cannot split one hot ordered partition automatically.

questions.question: How does a user-visible pending state reflect eventual consistency?
questions.answer: Pending states acknowledge durable acceptance while final cross-system evidence is incomplete; expose status/reconciliation rather than pretending immediate global atomicity.

questions.question: Why does a singleton cache need synchronization of compound operations?
questions.answer: Use one invariant-wide lock initially, or a carefully defined segmented/ownership policy that protects map membership and linked-list updates together.

questions.question: How do you evaluate a design choice when correctness and p99 latency conflict?
questions.answer: Treat required financial correctness as a constraint, then trade availability, asynchronous pending response, capacity and complexity to meet latency honestly. Do not silently violate the invariant to improve a percentile.

questions.question: The interviewer asks whether Kafka has exactly-once delivery and you claim yes for payments. How would you clarify the actual scope?
questions.answer: Limit the claim to supported Kafka transactional processing/offset-output boundaries with appropriate consumers. A bank can execute before a crash while local acknowledgement is lost. External operation identity, durable recovery and reconciliation remain necessary for one logical payment effect.

questions.question: An LRU cache works on one thread. Which interleavings would you test before declaring it thread-safe?
questions.answer: Test hit-versus-evict, two updates of one key, concurrent insert at capacity and callback reentry. Assert a valid linearized outcome, map/list bijection and neighbor symmetry under each forced schedule, using one correct structural lock as a baseline before attempting finer concurrency.

questions.question: A saga never finishes after a permanent provider failure. What operating procedure is missing?
questions.answer: Define a durable permanent-failure/noncompensable/manual-review state with owner, safe operator actions, evidence and retry/reconciliation limits. Alert on age and unresolved obligations. A workflow that merely stops scheduling after permanent failure is not an operable recovery design.

questions.question: If input is read-only, which parts of frequency selection can remain allocation-bound without mutating it?
questions.answer: Build separate frequency and candidate structures without modifying the input; grouping/heap allocation remains additional storage even though the array is read-only.

questions.question: How would you test output multiplicity to ensure a value is returned once rather than once per occurrence?
questions.answer: Assert output length equals the required distinct selection and that no value repeats; compare selected keys against a full-frequency oracle under the tie contract.

questions.question: Does placing HashMap entries directly into a heap create an aliasing risk if the map is later modified?
questions.answer: Yes if later mutation changes comparator-observed values or stored entries. Freeze counts/immutable pairs before heap construction, or update through an explicit reheapification protocol.

questions.question: During a timed re-solve, justify why the heap root is the first selected candidate to discard.
questions.answer: The root is the least desirable currently selected candidate by the frequency/tie comparator, so removing it preserves the best k among processed candidates.

questions.question: When choosing between buckets and a heap, which input constraints determine whether linear extra space is acceptable?
questions.answer: Input length n, distinct count u, requested k and allowed memory determine whether n+1 buckets are sensible versus O(k) heap selection state.

questions.question: How would a stable first-occurrence tie rule require metadata beyond just frequency?
questions.answer: Record each value's first input index and use it consistently in selection/tie ordering; counts alone cannot reconstruct encounter order.

questions.question: How do you prove a deduplication fix after consumer crash?
questions.answer: Kill/crash after business commit before progress acknowledgement, replay the original event and assert one durable effect and correct final consumer progress.

questions.question: What happens if a cache invalidation races with an update?
questions.answer: An old in-flight read can fill after invalidation, or a lost invalidation leaves stale copies. Use committed version/generation guards and durable invalidation recovery where required.

questions.question: How do you validate a token bucket refill invariant?
questions.answer: Use fake-time boundary tests and concurrent one-token/refill schedules, asserting nonnegative tokens, capacity saturation and admitted quota against elapsed time.

questions.question: Why does an integration test need a real transaction boundary?
questions.answer: Mocks do not execute unique/version constraints, rollback/commit boundaries, isolation, deadlocks or flush-time database errors. Use independent real connections/contexts and fresh post-completion assertions for the specific claimed invariant.

questions.question: What does a Kafka offset commit prove and not prove?
questions.answer: It records group partition progress, not proof that an arbitrary SQL/bank side effect completed atomically. Commit only safe contiguous completion.

questions.question: How do you reproduce a concurrency bug without flakiness?
questions.answer: Gate the relevant conflicting read/update phases, use independent worker state and await all outcomes, then assert the shared invariant under that forced interleaving.

questions.question: How do you explain a trade-off between LRU accuracy and throughput?
questions.answer: Exact global recency coordination can serialize a hot cache; approximate/segmented eviction may improve throughput while changing hit/eviction semantics. Measure and document that trade-off.

questions.question: What should a failed saga do after a non-retryable compensation?
questions.answer: Enter an explicit permanent/unknown/manual-reconciliation state with evidence and allowed repair actions; do not repeatedly issue unsafe compensation forever.

questions.question: Why should p99 service latency influence an LLD choice?
questions.answer: Locking, queues, callbacks and memory in an LLD can dominate the service's slowest requests, so validate relevant tails rather than only method-level Big-O.

questions.question: How can an idempotency table grow without limit?
questions.answer: Every new operation identity adds state. Partition/archive according to durable replay/audit horizons and capacity, not a short TTL that silently enables duplicates.

questions.question: An idempotent consumer test passes once but fails under replay. What durable record is missing?
questions.answer: The consumer lacks a durable processed/business identity committed atomically with its effect, or uses a new key on replay. Fix that boundary and test crash-after-commit/before-offset plus concurrent duplicate delivery; one successful delivery says nothing about replay safety.

questions.question: A token bucket test passes sequentially but fails with concurrent callers. Which critical section should be atomic?
questions.answer: Refill timestamp/token calculation, availability check and decrement must share one atomic state transition. Gate concurrent callers at an exact boundary and assert accepted count/capacity; merely synchronizing a counter without its elapsed-time state is incomplete.

questions.question: A Redis cache serves stale ledger amounts. What stronger read boundary is needed?
questions.answer: Use the authoritative ledger/transactionally verified operation state for financial decisions; allow cached balances only under an explicit safe read contract. Invalidate/fill by committed versions and reconcile drift. A longer/shorter Redis TTL cannot turn stale data into authoritative funds.

questions.question: How would a reference ArrayDeque plus explicit capacity validate random ring operations?
questions.answer: Generate seeded enqueue/dequeue/front/rear operations, limit reference size explicitly and compare results plus unchanged failure state after every operation, retaining a failing trace.

questions.question: If the queue grows dynamically, what order must be copied when head is not at index zero?
questions.answer: Copy logical FIFO positions old[(head+i)%oldCapacity] to new[i], then reset head=0 and derive tail/size under the new representation.

questions.question: Why is overwriting the oldest element a different contract from returning false when full?
questions.answer: Overwriting discards previously accepted unread data; rejection preserves it. These are different observable ownership/data-loss contracts, not interchangeable optimizations.

questions.question: During a cold re-solve, state the invariant relating head, size, capacity and logical element order.
questions.answer: The size live values appear in FIFO order starting at head modulo capacity, with 0<=size<=capacity and every next insertion/removal preserving that relation.

questions.question: A mocked repository returns success while a real unique constraint rejects the write. Which invariant must an integration test own?
questions.answer: The actual durable uniqueness and rollback/replay behavior under concurrent writers, including payload conflicts; mocks cannot supply the database's arbitration rule.

questions.question: A poisoned outbox record blocks every later record. Which quarantine and alert path permits safe progress?
questions.answer: Quarantine the classified record durably with original identity/error and alert on unresolved age; preserve aggregate ordering policy while allowing safe unrelated work to advance.

questions.question: A cache hit returns a mutable object changed by a caller. Which test proves value ownership rather than eviction order?
questions.answer: Mutate the returned value and original inserted object, then observe later reads. Assert the cache's chosen copy/immutable/shared-value contract independently of key eviction.

questions.question: A token-bucket stress test passes but never aligns calls at refill boundaries. Which deterministic interleaving remains untested?
questions.answer: Two callers must calculate/consume at the same last-token or exact-refill state. A lucky stress schedule may never align those reads before either writes.

questions.question: A saga terminates after a noncompensable provider step. What operator-visible recovery state and evidence are required?
questions.answer: Expose pending/unknown/manual reconciliation with original operation/provider references, step evidence, responsible owner and audited permitted correction actions.

questions.question: A dedupe marker expires before the allowed Kafka replay horizon. Which retention contract should prevent that mismatch?
questions.answer: Keep durable dedupe/operation tombstones through the maximum allowed replay plus reconciliation horizon; performance-cache TTL and credential expiry are separate policies.

questions.question: A consumer acknowledges an event in finally after a failed database operation. Which crash/replay test exposes the loss?
questions.answer: Crash after a failed/rolled-back DB action but after the finally offset commit; restart must reveal the skipped missing effect, proving premature acknowledgement loses work.

questions.question: A contract suite verifies request shape but not authentication scope. Which boundary remains uncovered?
questions.answer: The real authentication/authorization acceptance contract, including resource audience/scopes and provider credential behavior, still requires full boundary verification.

questions.question: A wallet transfer test checks totals but not tenant ownership. What negative case is still necessary?
questions.answer: Use a valid caller attempting another tenant's account/transfer and assert no unauthorized balance/journal mutation or data leakage, despite globally conserved totals.

questions.question: An LRU callback fails after eviction already committed. Which API result and retry semantics should the cache document?
questions.answer: Structural eviction already happened; specify callback failure independently, invocation/retry identity and backpressure. Retrying put/evict blindly must not repeat unrelated business effects.

questions.question: An outbox relay crashes between publish and acknowledgement. What reprocessing procedure is safe?
questions.answer: Resume publication with the same logical event identity and tolerate a possible already delivered record; the consumer deduplicates atomically with its effect. Keep retry/claim progress and operator scope durable. Do not manufacture a new event ID simply to avoid seeing an old send again.

questions.question: A mock system claims exactly-once settlement without a unique constraint. What test would disprove it?
questions.answer: Race or replay the same settlement reference through independent transactions/crash boundaries, then count/sum authoritative postings. Without a complete uniqueness/atomic state protocol it can duplicate; a local lock or one sequential green mock is not an exactly-once settlement proof.

questions.question: A saga fails after a noncompensable step. What manual-reconciliation state must exist?
questions.answer: Persist a noncompensable/unknown exception state with provider references, known committed steps, amount/currency and allowed auditable human actions. Assign ownership and alert on age. Corrections append history; they do not pretend the irreversible original action rolled back.

questions.question: What is the largest n permitted by the platform, and how should the return type be checked against that constraint?
questions.answer: The standard LeetCode 70 constraint is 1<=n<=45; ways(45)=F(46)=1,836,311,903 fits int. Wider/custom bounds need long/BigInteger or explicit overflow policy.

questions.question: How could a brute-force recursive enumerator verify small-n rolling-DP results?
questions.answer: Enumerate all 1/2-step paths for small n and compare their count with rolling DP. Keep the brute-force domain small because its exponential work is intentional.

questions.question: Why does caching only by n work for fixed step sizes but fail if the allowed-step set changes between calls?
questions.answer: n is sufficient only when the recurrence's allowed moves/seeds are fixed. Include every varying rule in the cache identity or isolate/reset the memo per problem instance.

questions.question: During a cold implementation, define exactly what dp[i] counts before writing its transition.
questions.answer: dp[i] is the number of ordered allowed-step sequences reaching exactly stair i, with explicit base/out-of-range/broken-stair policy.

questions.question: How does a Docker image differ from a container?
questions.answer: An image is an immutable, layered filesystem and execution configuration. A container is a running or stopped instance with a writable layer, isolated processes, networking and resource settings; many containers can share one image.

questions.question: What do image layers and a multi-stage build accomplish?
questions.answer: Layers allow content reuse and caching. Multi-stage builds compile and test with a full toolchain, then copy only required outputs into a smaller runtime stage; they do not automatically remove secrets copied into retained layers.

questions.question: Why should a container run as a non-root user?
questions.answer: A non-root UID reduces privileges available after compromise and accidental writes to system paths. Combine it with dropped capabilities, restricted mounts and host isolation; non-root alone is not a complete sandbox.

questions.question: How do cgroup memory limits affect a Java process?
questions.answer: The kernel accounts and limits container memory through cgroups. Modern container-aware JVMs size ergonomics using detected limits, but heap is only part of usage: stacks, metaspace, buffers and native allocations also count.

questions.question: What is the difference between COPY and ADD?
questions.answer: COPY copies build-context files or outputs from another stage. ADD also supports features such as local archive extraction and remote sources. Prefer COPY when those extra semantics are unnecessary, making builds easier to audit.

questions.question: How do Docker bridge networks connect containers?
questions.answer: A bridge provides a virtual network linking container interfaces through the host. User-defined bridge networks support container-name DNS; publishing a port exposes a service outside that network, subject to host and firewall configuration.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a health check in a container?
questions.answer: It reports whether the application can perform a defined check, rather than merely whether its process exists. Docker health status alone does not guarantee automatic restart or Kubernetes probe behavior; the orchestrator needs its own policy.

questions.question: How do you keep secrets out of a Docker image?
questions.answer: Use build secret mounts for temporary build credentials and runtime secret injection for application credentials. Exclude secret files from context, avoid ARG/ENV embedding and prevent application or build commands from copying secrets into outputs.

questions.question: What happens to local container state when it is recreated?
questions.answer: The recreated container starts with a fresh writable layer, so unmounted changes disappear. Volumes, external databases and object stores have separate lifecycles; a simple process restart within the same container need not erase its layer.

questions.question: How would you reduce the attack surface of a Java runtime image?
questions.answer: Use a supported minimal runtime image, pinned dependencies, a non-root user and only necessary libraries. Consider jlink where module compatibility permits; scan and rebuild regularly, and retain a workable diagnostics strategy.

questions.question: What is the purpose of .dockerignore?
questions.answer: It excludes unnecessary or sensitive files from the build context, reducing transfer, cache invalidation and accidental COPY exposure. It complements secret management; it cannot remove a secret already present in a published image.

questions.question: Why use an explicit image digest?
questions.answer: A digest identifies exact image content, preventing a mutable tag from resolving to different bytes between environments. Record signatures, provenance and vulnerability status as well; immutability alone does not establish trust or ongoing safety.

questions.question: How does a read-only filesystem limit damage?
questions.answer: A read-only root filesystem prevents many persistence and modification paths. Explicit writable temporary directories or volumes remain necessary; it does not prevent network exfiltration or writes to permitted mounts and external services.

questions.question: How do you provide JVM options through environment variables?
questions.answer: Set JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS or JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS for supported launcher behavior, or have an entrypoint explicitly construct arguments. JAVA_OPTS is only a convention unless a script consumes it. Check quoting and avoid exposing secrets in options.

questions.question: A container is OOMKilled with heap remaining. How would you investigate off-heap and memory-limit interaction?
questions.answer: Confirm exit reason and cgroup memory events, then compare RSS/container usage with heap, direct buffers, thread count and metaspace. Enable Native Memory Tracking in a reproducible run and examine untracked native/page-cache usage. Leave measured headroom and limit concurrency; increasing Xmx can worsen this failure.

questions.question: A secret is embedded in an image layer and removed in a later layer. Why is the leak still present?
questions.answer: Image layers retain earlier filesystem contents; later deletion generally adds a whiteout, not secure erasure. Revoke or rotate the credential immediately, identify published copies and rebuild without the secret using build mounts. Remove accessible compromised artifacts according to policy; rebuilding alone does not invalidate stolen credentials.

questions.question: A restart loses files written by the application. How would you redesign persistent state?
questions.answer: Classify files as disposable cache, durable business data or required configuration. Put durable data in an appropriate database, object store or managed volume with backup and recovery tests. Keep containers replaceable and handle concurrent writers explicitly; merely mounting a directory does not provide replication or transactional correctness.

questions.question: Can Union-Find solve static island counting, and what extra structure is paid for relative to DFS?
questions.answer: Yes. Assign each land cell a parent and union four-neighbor land cells; count distinct roots or decrement an initial component count on successful unions. Parent/rank arrays add O(rows*cols) storage beyond the grid.

questions.question: How does dynamically adding land differ from recounting a fixed grid after every update?
questions.answer: Maintain a Union-Find structure across additions: add one component for new land, then merge distinct neighboring components. Ignore duplicate additions. This avoids traversing the entire fixed grid after every update; deletions require a more complex approach.

questions.question: For a checkerboard grid, what is the maximum number of four-connected islands?
questions.answer: For a nonempty m-by-n grid, ceil(m*n/2) isolated land cells are achievable with alternating cells under four-connectivity. A one-cell grid yields one; an empty dimension yields zero.

questions.question: How would a reference BFS and a DFS implementation cross-check results on small randomly generated grids?
questions.answer: Generate small rectangular binary grids with a fixed seed. Clone each input for mutating traversals, compare island counts from independently written BFS and DFS, and include all-water, all-land, single-row and diagonal-only cases.

questions.question: Why can splitting a grid into independently counted tiles overcount islands crossing tile borders?
questions.answer: One island can occupy cells in several tiles, so adding local counts counts that component repeatedly. Connectivity crosses the partition boundary even though each tile's internal traversal is correct.

questions.question: Which border-component information would parallel tile processing need to merge?
questions.answer: Give local components unique tile-qualified IDs and expose component IDs for boundary land cells. Union IDs of neighboring land cells across tile edges, then subtract successful merges from local totals; handle all boundaries exactly once.
