questions.question: A collision-heavy HashMap benchmark improves after resizing; how would you distinguish shorter chains from actual treeification?
questions.answer: Inspect bucket lengths/capacity and actual node representation in a controlled benchmark, using suitable tooling for the exact JDK. Separate improved hash distribution after resize from tree-bin conversion; timing alone does not prove which mechanism occurred.

questions.question: Why can CompletableFuture.runAsync lose transaction context?
questions.answer: Imperative Spring transactions are normally bound to the calling thread. runAsync executes elsewhere without inheriting that connection/transaction context. Invoke a proxied transactional worker for a new transaction or redesign the asynchronous unit and its consistency boundary.

questions.question: How do N+1 fetches appear under a page-size increase?
questions.answer: An initial page query is followed by extra association queries per returned entity, so SQL count and latency grow with page size. Measure actual SQL and access paths; batching/caching can change the slope and fetch joins can introduce different row-multiplication costs.

questions.question: A refunded-event replay arrives after a newer cancellation event; how must version checks interact with deduplication?
questions.answer: Deduplicate event identity and independently enforce aggregate version plus permitted transitions. A distinct older refunded event must not overwrite newer authoritative cancellation/correction state; reconcile conflicts where the provider lifecycle is not a simple total order.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a bounded executor under load?
questions.answer: A bounded pool/queue limits retained work and exposes overload through admission delay or rejection. Choose a clear rejection/backpressure policy and shared deadline; an unbounded queue can hide saturation until latency and memory become unacceptable.

questions.question: How can a circuit breaker protect a slow notification provider?
questions.answer: A breaker stops or limits calls after classified failures/slow calls, allowing recovery probes later. Pair it with timeouts, bulkheads and rate limits; it does not cancel existing provider work or guarantee a timed-out send did not occur.

questions.question: Why does a composite index's order change plan selection?
questions.answer: Index column order affects usable range, ordering and scan work under a query's predicates and engine behavior. Evaluate selectivity, leading constraints, statistics and skip-scan possibilities; inspect the actual plan rather than applying a universal prefix slogan.

questions.question: How do you verify token bucket correctness under contention?
questions.answer: Use a fake monotonic clock, synchronize contenders at a known boundary and assert total grants never exceed available tokens. Test refill once per elapsed interval, capacity clamping and concurrent failure paths; the refill-and-consume transition must be atomic.

questions.question: Why is an idempotency key not sufficient without durable storage?
questions.answer: A key held only in memory/cache disappears on restart, eviction or failover, and replicas may disagree. Enforce uniqueness and operation/result state in durable shared storage with the financial effect, retaining it for the actual retry/replay horizon.

questions.question: Your cache design saves heap by evicting large values first; how does that policy differ from strict LRU and what contract changes?
questions.answer: Evicting large values first is a size-aware policy, not strict least-recently-used ordering. Document byte weights, admission, recency interaction and oversized-entry behavior; benchmark hit-rate/cost consequences rather than preserving an inaccurate LRU label.

questions.question: Your cache exercise adds a mutable value shared by two callers. Which ownership contract and concurrency test should accompany the change?
questions.answer: Choose immutable values, defensive copies or explicitly synchronized shared mutation. Test two callers obtaining the same cached object, then mutate one under controlled ordering and assert the chosen isolation/visibility contract. Correct map/list locking cannot protect an arbitrary value after it is returned to callers.

questions.question: A Spring/JPA mock reveals a transaction boundary mistake. What failing integration test would you add?
questions.answer: Call the actual proxied entry point against a real test database, force failure after the first write and verify from a separate transaction that no partial effect remains. Include the self-call/async/propagation path that was wrong; a mocked repository cannot prove commit behavior.

questions.question: A Kafka interview probes exactly-once guarantees. How do you distinguish event handling from bank side effects?
questions.answer: Kafka transactions can atomically cover supported Kafka reads/writes and offsets within their scope, but not an arbitrary bank debit or SQL transaction. Show the crash after bank success and before local/Kafka completion, then explain durable identity, provider idempotency and reconciliation for that external uncertainty.

questions.question: What difference does TTL introduce beyond pure least-recently-used eviction?
questions.answer: TTL introduces time-based validity independent of recency: the most recently used entry can still expire. Define expiry clock, lazy/eager removal, refresh behavior and whether access extends TTL; recency eviction alone does not enforce freshness.

questions.question: If a read returns a mutable cached value, what ownership problem remains despite correct eviction logic?
questions.answer: Callers can mutate the same object or race after get returns, regardless of correct eviction. Define immutable/copy/shared ownership and synchronization; an evicted object can also remain live while a caller holds its reference.

questions.question: Why can invoking a user callback while holding the cache lock create a reentrancy or deadlock risk?
questions.answer: The callback may call back into the cache, block or acquire another lock in reverse order. Collect callback events under the lock and invoke after release, with documented ordering and exception handling.

questions.question: What happens if capacity is reduced below current size at runtime?
questions.answer: Evict according to the defined policy until size<=newCapacity, atomically with the capacity change. Define zero/negative capacity and callback behavior, and ensure concurrent puts cannot temporarily violate the new bound without a stated allowance.

questions.question: A mock answer describes a successful flush as durable commit. Which later rollback trace would correct that claim?
questions.answer: Persist and flush an entity, then throw a rollback-triggering exception before transaction completion. Query through a separate connection after rollback and show the row is absent; flushed SQL participated in a transaction and was not yet a durable commit.

questions.question: A project story lacks a preserved baseline. How would you qualify the impact and still explain the concrete engineering decision?
questions.answer: State the actual observed behavior and architectural mechanism, acknowledge the missing baseline and omit unverifiable precision. Support your decision with surviving plans, traces, tests or operational records and propose a fair new comparison if needed.

questions.question: A consumer commits offsets after dispatching to workers. Which outstanding lower-offset work must finish before that commit is safe?
questions.answer: All records below the committed next offset must have completed their durable effects, including every lower-offset asynchronous task. Commit only the contiguous completed prefix; dispatched or highest-seen is not equivalent to completed.

questions.question: A virtual-thread design bounds JDBC calls but permits unlimited queued requests. Which memory/admission risk remains?
questions.answer: Unlimited admitted requests can retain payloads, thread-local data, futures and deadlines while waiting for JDBC permits. Bound total in-flight work and queue age as well as database concurrency; cheap virtual threads do not eliminate memory limits.

questions.question: A permission test authenticates a user but never changes tenant ID. Which authorization defect could still pass?
questions.answer: Cross-tenant object access can still pass because the test never changes resource ownership. Authenticate tenant A and request tenant B's resource, asserting denial and no leakage/side effect even with a cryptographically valid token.

questions.question: A stale cache is allowed for status reads but used to approve a debit. Which contract boundary has been crossed?
questions.answer: An informational freshness contract was used for a financial authorization decision. Debit approval must consult authoritative balance/invariants transactionally; a stale status cache is not a permissible substitute for that authority.

questions.question: A saga compensation can succeed twice if retried. Which compensating-operation identity makes that safe?
questions.answer: Give the compensation a stable identity derived from saga/step/purpose and enforce its durable uniqueness with the compensating financial posting. Retrying a refund must retrieve the prior result rather than create another credit.

questions.question: A Kafka producer restart uses the same transactional.id. Which fencing event should the timeline explain?
questions.answer: The new producer instance obtains a newer epoch and fences the old instance for that transactional.id. Explain detection/handling of the stale producer's failure and why the ID must match the intended ownership scope rather than be shared by concurrent legitimate producers.

questions.question: A code mock passes because a reference solution was memorized but fails on changed null semantics. Which contract should be restated before coding?
questions.answer: Restate allowed null/empty inputs, mutation, ordering, duplicate handling and failure behavior before selecting an algorithm. A memorized implementation only applies under its original contract; adapt tests to the newly specified semantics.

questions.question: A recovery diagram includes a manual step with no evidence trail. Which audit record and ownership make the procedure operable?
questions.answer: Record the authorized operator, reason, affected operation IDs, evidence, commands/changes, before/after validation and timestamps. Assign a responsible owner and escalation path, with least privilege and independent review where financial policy requires it.

questions.question: An LLD mock challenges thread safety of an LRU cache. What interleaving would you illustrate?
questions.answer: Thread A looks up node X, thread B evicts X and unlinks it, then A moves its stale node to MRU. The list can contain an entry absent from the map or damaged links. Put lookup, membership validation and recency/eviction mutations under one lock for the baseline.

questions.question: A project claims a 40% p99 improvement, but the baseline traffic was half the new load. How would you present the evidence and design a fair comparison?
questions.answer: Present both observed load conditions and say the 40% comparison is confounded. Re-run old/new versions under matched offered load, dataset, resources, warmup and error accounting, ideally alternating runs. Report p99 with throughput/rejections and uncertainty; improved performance at higher load is encouraging evidence, not a controlled causal percentage.

questions.question: A system design mock introduces a downstream outage. What graceful-degradation rule would you defend?
questions.answer: Preserve correctness first: allow declared stale informational reads or durable asynchronous acceptance only where contractually valid, and reject/pend balance-changing operations whose authority is unavailable. Bound retries, isolate dependency capacity and expose unknown outcomes honestly; degradation should not invent successful financial confirmation.

questions.question: Why does removing a matched value from the membership set prevent duplicate output during the second scan?
questions.answer: Set.remove returns true only for the first matching occurrence. After removal, later duplicate values in the second array cannot emit that value again, satisfying distinct intersection without a separate output set.

questions.question: What changes if the required output is the multiset intersection with repeated values?
questions.answer: Use value-to-count frequencies and emit a value while the remaining count is positive, decrementing on each match. Output multiplicity becomes min(countA,countB), so removing the entire value after one match is incorrect.

questions.question: How would a two-pointer intersection avoid returning the same value twice from duplicate runs?
questions.answer: When equal values match, emit once and advance both pointers past all copies of that value. On inequality advance only the smaller side, also optionally skipping its duplicate run.

questions.question: If one array is stored on disk and the other fits in memory, which access pattern is practical?
questions.answer: Build a set from the in-memory array and scan the disk array sequentially, removing matched values to suppress duplicates. Sequential I/O avoids random disk lookups; if neither fits, consider external sorting or partitioning with explicit resource costs.

days.focus: Audit two weakest backend failure cases for 20 minutes; build one discriminating proof in 30 minutes and log remaining uncertainty.

questions.question: A payment row exists but no event was published; which transaction/relay boundaries would you reconstruct?
questions.answer: Reconstruct whether business row and outbox row committed together, relay polling/locking, publish attempts, broker acknowledgments and completion marking. If no outbox intent existed in the transaction, identify the commit-before-publish gap rather than blaming delivery alone.

questions.question: Two pods both accept one idempotency key; show the database operation that arbitrates the winner.
questions.answer: Use a database unique constraint on (tenant_id, operation_type, idempotency_key) and attempt an insert carrying the request fingerprint. One commit establishes ownership; the other path reads/replays or reports an in-progress/conflict result according to database transaction semantics.

questions.question: After a GC cycle the live set keeps growing; which retention evidence separates a leak from a larger legitimate cache?
questions.answer: Compare post-GC retained growth with cache entry/weight limits, workload cardinality and dominator/reference paths. A legitimate cache should have a documented bounded retention policy; a growing owner chain or entries outside intended lifecycle suggests a leak.

questions.question: A service returns stale status only after a failed transaction; how would you correlate cache invalidation with commit events?
questions.answer: Align transaction outcome, outbox/invalidation event, cache key/version and read source in traces/logs. Invalidation before commit or unconditional repopulation on rollback can publish stale/wrong values; tie changes to committed state and handle retryable invalidation durably.

questions.question: A query starts spilling after a data-distribution change; which estimated and actual plan rows matter?
questions.answer: Compare estimated versus actual rows at filters, joins and aggregation/sort nodes, including skewed bind values, row widths and memory/spill settings. Stale statistics or changed correlation can create large intermediate results despite a previously acceptable plan.

questions.question: An offset is committed while one async handler is still running; what can be lost after a crash?
questions.answer: The committed offset can skip that unfinished record after restart, permanently losing its business effect unless another durable recovery path exists. Offsets must follow completed durable work, not task dispatch or future creation.

questions.question: A singleton has a request-specific mutable field; construct a two-request interference trace.
questions.answer: Request A stores accountA in the singleton, B overwrites with accountB, then A uses the field and acts on B. Move request state to method-local immutable arguments and test the interleaving with latches.

questions.question: The application reports 403 while the browser reports CORS failure; how would you separate the two paths?
questions.answer: Inspect the actual preflight and business requests separately in network/server logs. CORS can prevent the browser exposing a 403 response; fix allowed-origin/header/preflight configuration and independently verify authentication/resource authorization rather than interpreting the browser message as the root cause.

questions.question: Why can retrying an unknown bank response create a second debit even if the local transaction rolled back?
questions.answer: The bank is outside the local database transaction and may have committed before its response was lost. Local rollback cannot undo it. Preserve the external identity and reconcile/query before retrying; a new request identity can create another debit.

questions.question: An optimistic-lock retry runs inside a rollback-only persistence context; why must the transaction boundary change?
questions.answer: Rollback-only cannot be cleared into a valid retry, and the persistence context may contain stale/failed state. Start a fresh transaction/context and repeat the entire business calculation with fresh data, preserving logical operation identity.

questions.question: If trace sampling drops most successes, which metrics still measure overall error rate and latency?
questions.answer: Unsampled request counters, error counters and latency histograms should measure all relevant attempts/outcomes. Sampled traces support diagnosis but their selected population cannot automatically estimate unbiased overall error rates or latency distributions.

questions.question: How would an expand-and-contract migration support consumers using two schema versions?
questions.answer: Add fields/tables and tolerant readers first, support old and new representations during migration, backfill and validate, then switch and remove only after all consumers and rollback windows permit. Version event/schema contracts independently where necessary.

questions.question: A pool is half idle while one partition lags; which per-partition or hot-key constraint could explain it?
questions.answer: A single partition, hot aggregate, ordered handler or slow record can serialize work while other pool capacity sits idle. Inspect per-partition lag/service time and key skew; more general worker threads cannot split an ordering constraint safely by themselves.

questions.question: In a payment design, which operations must sacrifice availability when the balance source cannot be reached?
questions.answer: Reject or leave pending operations requiring authoritative available balance, unique payment claims or ledger invariant checks when those cannot be established. Continue independently safe reads/acceptance only with explicit freshness/durability semantics; availability must not mean inventing money correctness.

questions.question: A blue/green deployment routes repeat requests to different database schemas. Design an idempotency boundary that survives the transition.
questions.answer: Keep a shared durable operation registry/ledger authority across versions or migrate it with explicitly compatible ownership and routing. Enforce tenant-scoped uniqueness and request fingerprints there, preserve keys across green/blue traffic and replays, and test concurrent requests spanning both versions. Separate databases with independent keys cannot arbitrate one payment safely by themselves.

questions.question: A nightly reconciliation finds debits without matching credits after an async refactor. Which transaction and event traces would you collect before repair?
questions.answer: Freeze unsafe retries and collect operation IDs, ledger transactions, connection/commit boundaries, outbox/inbox events, offsets, versions and provider references. Identify whether a formerly atomic debit/credit was split or an effect was skipped/replayed. Repair using audited balancing entries after authoritative reconciliation, preserving original evidence and verifying control totals.

questions.question: A payment service has high p99 with normal average CPU and heap. Design the first fifteen minutes of evidence collection.
questions.answer: First confirm affected routes, regions, versions, timeout rate and p99 windows. Then capture executor/JDBC queue time, dependency traces, lock waits, thread dumps and GC/safepoints with synchronized timestamps. Correlate deployments and retry amplification, preserve one affected instance and choose a bounded mitigation; normal average CPU/heap does not exclude waiting or pauses.

questions.question: Why does sorting a char[] preserve the original immutable String but still allocate memory?
questions.answer: String is immutable, so toCharArray creates a separate mutable array that sorting can rearrange safely. The array still consumes O(n) extra memory, plus sorting machinery; immutability of the source does not make the operation allocation-free.

questions.question: If a library changes from case-sensitive to case-insensitive anagrams, what regression tests should preserve the old API behavior?
questions.answer: Keep explicit tests showing "a" versus "A" is false for the old case-sensitive API, and add a separately named/versioned case-insensitive contract if compatibility matters. Test locale/Unicode policy deliberately rather than silently changing normalization.

questions.question: Design a property test: permuting a string must preserve its anagram equivalence class.
questions.answer: Generate a string, randomly shuffle its characters under the same alphabet model and assert the checker returns true. Then alter a character/count and assert false where guaranteed; use a fixed seed and include repeated/empty inputs.

questions.question: Show that anagram equality is symmetric and transitive; which careless normalization rule could violate consistency?
questions.answer: Canonical equality is symmetric and transitive because both sides use the same deterministic normalization and multiset representation. Applying different locale, truncation or normalization rules depending on argument position breaks that equivalence contract.

questions.question: Explain how a mismatch at the last character tests that the entire second string is examined.
questions.answer: Use equal-length strings sharing all but the final counted character, such as "ab" and "ac". Code that stops before the final character may falsely accept; assert false and test final-position differences with repeated prefixes too.

questions.question: Reimplement anagram checking without sorting and report separately the cost in input length and alphabet size.
questions.answer: Count the first string and decrement for the second, rejecting mismatches under a defined alphabet. Time is O(n+m+A) if initializing/scanning A counters; space is O(A), constant only when the alphabet is fixed.

questions.question: Write the schema and insert path for a tenant-scoped idempotency reservation with a payload fingerprint.
questions.answer: Create a primary/unique key on tenant, operation type and idempotency key, storing request fingerprint, status, operation ID and result. Insert in the effect's transaction; on conflict compare fingerprints and replay or report in-progress. The accompanying SQL sketch shows the arbitration point.

questions.question: Sketch a transaction-scoped debit update that rejects insufficient funds without a stale read-check-write gap.
questions.answer: Use an atomic conditional debit, for example UPDATE account SET balance=balance-:amount, version=version+1 WHERE id=:id AND balance>=:amount. Validate positive amount/currency and require update count one; write the balanced journal in the same transaction. Add a version predicate when that contract is required.

questions.question: Implement an outbox insert beside a ledger journal and identify which connection must perform both.
questions.answer: Insert journal rows and the outbox intent using the same transaction-managed connection/DataSource transaction. If either insert fails, roll back both. A second autocommit connection would recreate the gap; the relay publishes later and consumers still deduplicate.

questions.question: Write a bounded async fan-out skeleton that shares one request deadline across dependencies.
questions.answer: Create one monotonic deadline, admit only bounded work and pass remaining time to every dependency. Cancel unfinished futures at expiry and ensure clients enforce transport deadlines. The code sketch demonstrates composition boundaries; logical cancellation alone does not prove physical I/O stopped.

questions.question: Show a JPA projection query that retrieves an order summary without lazy serialization.
questions.answer: Use a constructor/interface projection selecting only required scalar fields, such as order ID, customer display name and total. Return the projection DTO directly rather than an entity graph whose serializer traverses lazy associations; the example includes an explicit join.

questions.question: Write a two-connection test for an optimistic-lock conflict and state which final state is acceptable.
questions.answer: Use two independent EntityManagers/transactions loading version v, coordinate both reads, then commit one update before the other flushes/commits. Exactly one conflicting stale update should fail; verify one legitimate final value/version through a fresh transaction and retry the loser only as a new unit of work.

questions.question: Implement a retry classifier that separates permanent validation errors from transient transport failures.
questions.answer: Classify validation/authentication and business-rule failures as permanent; classify selected transient transport/service failures as eligible only within a deadline/attempt budget and idempotency policy. Unknown external outcomes require reconciliation, not automatic retry merely because the exception is a timeout.

questions.question: Sketch a cache loader that permits one active load per key and removes failed loads.
questions.answer: Use a ConcurrentHashMap<Key,CompletableFuture<Value>> for in-flight ownership: putIfAbsent a placeholder, let the winner load outside map callbacks, complete it and remove(key, sameFuture) in finally. Decide separately how successful values enter the cache and how executor rejection completes waiters.

questions.question: Write a Spring test configuration for a library with no main application class.
questions.answer: Declare a test @Configuration with explicit @Import of the library configuration and test collaborators, then point @SpringBootTest(classes=...) at it. Add minimal auto-configuration/properties only as required; no host application main class or accidental broad scan is needed.

questions.question: Show a deterministic race test using latches, including a timeout so a defect cannot hang the suite.
questions.answer: Use phase latches/barriers to force the hazardous ordering, not just simultaneous starts, and await each phase with a timeout. Capture worker exceptions, release gates in finally and assert a final invariant. The included test intentionally reproduces a lost update deterministically.

questions.question: Write a keyset query ordered by created_at and id, including the tie predicate for the cursor.
questions.answer: Use WHERE created_at>:time OR (created_at=:time AND id>:id), ORDER BY created_at,id and LIMIT :size for ascending non-null keys. Define a snapshot/concurrent-write policy and cursor validation; descending order requires reversing both comparisons and ordering.

questions.question: Implement a Kafka dedupe insert and business update under one local database transaction.
questions.answer: Insert a unique consumer/event dedupe row and apply the business update with the same database transaction. On conflict skip only a previously completed committed effect. Acknowledge/commit Kafka offsets afterward; if the transaction rolls back, the dedupe reservation must roll back too.

questions.question: Sketch the CI gate that tests a migration against a previous-release database snapshot.
questions.answer: Restore a sanitized previous-release schema/data snapshot in isolation, apply the candidate migration, run old/new compatibility checks and validate invariants/control totals. Publish logs and gate the immutable artifact; a schema-only empty database cannot reveal all migration/data problems.

questions.question: Write a token-bucket test with a fake clock for an exact boundary refill.
questions.answer: With capacity two and rate one token/second, consume both at fake time zero, assert rejection at 999,999,999 ns and one grant at 1,000,000,000 ns. Also assert no double refill at the same timestamp; do not use Thread.sleep for this boundary test.

questions.question: Implement a minimal payment state machine and test an out-of-order success callback after a timeout. Which transitions require compare-and-set persistence?
questions.answer: Model CREATED -> PENDING, client timeout as still UNKNOWN/PENDING, and verified success as SUCCEEDED; timeout is not a conflicting financial terminal failure. Persist versioned conditional transitions and operation identity, and test duplicate/late callbacks. Use compare-and-set/version checks wherever response, callback and reconciliation can race to change authoritative state.

questions.question: Build a two-request duplicate-charge reproduction with a real database constraint; what outcome proves one winner and one replay?
questions.answer: Run two real database transactions with the same tenant/key and fingerprint, forcing overlap. Assert one durable payment/effect and one replay or defined in-progress response, never two provider identities. Include a changed-payload conflict and crash/retry case; verify committed state from a fresh connection rather than only HTTP responses.

questions.question: Rebuild a bounded fan-out demo that cancels unfinished work at a deadline; how will you prove downstream work actually stops?
questions.answer: Use bounded admission, one deadline and cancellable clients/tasks. At expiry cancel unfinished handles, then verify active task count, client connections and downstream server observations fall to the expected bound within a grace period. A cancelled/done Future alone proves only handle state, not stopped network work.

questions.question: Construct a FIFO property test comparing operation sequences against ArrayDeque.
questions.answer: Generate enqueue/dequeue/peek sequences and execute them on the two-stack queue and an ArrayDeque model. Compare each result and size, including empty behavior and long alternating bursts; use deterministic seeds and assert rather than print.

questions.question: If the API needs bounded capacity, which size invariant must be checked across both stacks?
questions.answer: Check inputStack.size()+outputStack.size() < capacity before accepting an enqueue, atomically with the push in a concurrent API. Counting only the input stack permits overflow while older elements still wait in the output stack.

questions.question: What changes when dequeue should throw on empty versus return an optional result?
questions.answer: Choose one explicit empty contract, such as NoSuchElementException or OptionalInt.empty, and apply it consistently to peek/dequeue. Internal transfer logic is unchanged; avoid value sentinels when every integer is valid input.

questions.question: How can forgetting to remove a transferred input element create duplicates in later queue outputs?
questions.answer: Copying peeked values without popping leaves them in the input stack, so a later transfer enqueues the same elements again. Transfer using output.push(input.pop()) and assert each accepted element is removed exactly once.

questions.question: If only one stack is permitted, why does using recursion still consume an implicit second stack?
questions.answer: Recursion stores deferred elements in call frames, which are another stack in memory. It therefore does not satisfy a true constant-extra-space one-stack restriction and can overflow at large queue sizes.

questions.question: Rebuild the two-stack queue and explain how it handles an input/output-stack state where both are nonempty.
questions.answer: New values push onto input; dequeue/peek use output while it is nonempty. Only when output empties do you reverse all input elements into it. Both stacks can be nonempty because older output values must leave before newer input values.

days.focus: Triage two failure cases for 10 minutes each; implement one repair in 30 minutes and record the other in the backlog.

questions.question: After deployment, readiness passes but all business requests fail; which health-check dependency was omitted?
questions.answer: The probe may validate only process/port availability while required initialization, schema compatibility or a mandatory dependency is unusable. Identify the actual failing request stage and define readiness for promised traffic without turning shared dependency failures into restart cascades.

questions.question: Bank timeouts rise while the circuit remains closed; how could result classification or a large sample window hide the problem?
questions.answer: Timeout exceptions may be ignored/misclassified, asynchronous failures may occur outside the measured call, or minimum-call/window settings may dilute the signal. Inspect recorded outcomes and slow-call thresholds against real traffic; also ensure calls actually pass through the breaker.

questions.question: Consumer lag falls to zero while the SQL table stops changing; which swallowed-error or premature-commit path would you inspect?
questions.answer: Inspect swallowed exceptions, completion-before-commit, offsets committed at dispatch and dedupe rows written separately from effects. Lag zero means the consumer advanced offsets, not that business updates succeeded. Compare event IDs and durable transaction outcomes.

questions.question: An outbox row is published repeatedly but never marked complete; how do you distinguish relay failure from an acknowledgement loss?
questions.answer: Correlate stable event ID, broker acknowledgments, relay logs and database completion updates. Crash after publish but before marking complete causes legitimate republish; missing/uncertain acknowledgments can do the same. Consumers must deduplicate rather than treating relay status as exactly-once proof.

questions.question: An API latency histogram looks healthy although timeouts increase; which missing measurements could bias it?
questions.answer: It may exclude rejected, timed-out or never-completed requests, measure only handler time or use wrong bucket/query windows. Compare edge end-to-end metrics and total offered/completed/error counts; successful-only latency can look healthy during severe failure.

questions.question: A paginated fetch join silently returns fewer root entities; how would row multiplication appear in the actual SQL result?
questions.answer: One root with many children produces many SQL rows, so applying row limits can truncate root coverage or trigger in-memory pagination. Inspect generated SQL and actual root IDs/row counts; use a two-step ID page or projection appropriate to the required graph.

questions.question: After a JVM upgrade, a native library stalls virtual threads; which controlled comparison isolates the library from database capacity?
questions.answer: Compare platform versus virtual threads on the same JDK/library and fixed load, with a controlled fake dependency replacing JDBC. Capture JFR/native stacks and vary only the suspect library/JDK boundary. Pinning behavior differs by JDK; do not infer native compatibility from a database-saturated benchmark.

questions.question: One tenant monopolizes a shared executor; which admission and fairness boundaries would you introduce?
questions.answer: Introduce per-tenant admission/concurrency quotas, bounded queues and fair scheduling or dedicated bulkheads for important classes. Keep a global resource cap and deadline; separate pools alone can still overload a shared downstream database.

questions.question: A database migration waits for a metadata lock during a release; what session evidence should guide mitigation?
questions.answer: Identify blocker and waiter sessions, lock types/objects, transaction age, DDL timeout and application activity using supported engine views. Pause the rollout and assess whether safely completing/cancelling a blocker or rescheduling DDL is preferable; indiscriminate session killing can worsen recovery.

questions.question: A mutable composite key changes after insertion; how could rebuilding the map reveal stranded entries?
questions.answer: Iteration can still find entries whose cached insertion hash no longer matches the mutated key. Re-inserting into a fresh map recomputes current hashes and may restore lookup, revealing the violation; it can merge newly equal keys, so it is diagnostic, not a substitute for immutable keys.

questions.question: A contract test validates required fields but misses a new enum value; what consumer behavior should be tested?
questions.answer: Test how old consumers handle unknown enum values: reject with a clear contract error, map to an explicit UNKNOWN or tolerate/preserve them as specified. Required-field validation alone misses semantic expansion and strict deserializer failures.

questions.question: Docker image scanning passes while a secret remains in an old layer; which build and credential changes are required?
questions.answer: Rotate/revoke the exposed credential, rebuild without the secret using secret mounts/runtime injection and address accessible compromised artifacts. A vulnerability scanner is not a guarantee of secret detection, and later-layer deletion does not erase earlier content.

questions.question: A settlement rerun has the correct record count but the wrong total amount; which per-record and aggregate checks isolate the discrepancy?
questions.answer: Compare per-record amount/currency/scale, duplicate/missing references, signs, fees and adjustment versions, then totals by currency and debit/credit class. Correct row count can hide one missing and one duplicated row or parsing/rounding errors; use independent statement control totals.

questions.question: A cache metric reports a 99% hit rate while p99 degrades; which hot-key, stale-hit or miss-coalescing evidence would you seek?
questions.answer: Break down hit/miss latency, key skew, value sizes, stale-hit rate, loader concurrency and database fallback time. A small number of expensive hot-key misses can dominate p99 despite high aggregate hit rate; coalescing and freshness semantics matter as much as the percentage.

questions.question: A rollback deployed old code against a schema with a dropped column. How would you contain failures and redesign migration rollback safety?
questions.answer: Stop further rollout and route to a compatible version or forward-fix path; assess whether restoring a compatibility column is safe without inventing lost data. Preserve evidence and reconcile failed operations. Redesign releases with additive expansion, a tested rollback window and delayed destructive contraction, including old-code compatibility tests against the migrated schema.

questions.question: A Kafka event is retried after the recipient bank already executed its effect. What external reference and reconciliation process can resolve uncertainty?
questions.answer: Recover using the original merchant/payment operation identity and provider reference, not a fresh retry ID. Query provider status and compare callbacks/settlement evidence, then apply the local result and journal once. If no reference returned, require lookup by the original idempotency/merchant key or explicitly escalate the unknown outcome.

questions.question: A connection-pool increase doubles database lock waits. How would you reverse the change and measure safe concurrency?
questions.answer: Return to the prior safe pool/concurrency setting with controlled rollout, then measure database lock waits, transaction service time, throughput and tail latency under representative load. Test a concurrency sweep and cap admission near sustainable capacity; more connections can increase contention without adding useful throughput.

questions.question: How would you property-test a search result against linear membership without demanding a fixed duplicate index?
questions.answer: Use linear membership as the oracle. If absent, assert -1; if present, assert the returned index is in range and a[index]==target. With duplicates, any matching index is valid unless the contract specifically requires first/last.

questions.question: Why can an array concurrently reordered by another thread invalidate binary search even when each read is atomic?
questions.answer: Binary search requires one consistent sorted sequence throughout the operation. Atomic individual reads do not provide a snapshot or preserve order across steps; synchronize mutation/search or search an immutable snapshot under the defined ownership contract.

questions.question: What boundary tests distinguish target below all elements from target above all elements?
questions.answer: For [2,4,6], target1 and target7 must both return -1 without out-of-bounds access. Also test equality at2/6, empty input and a singleton to expose incorrect lower/upper bound updates.

questions.question: Reconstruct the algorithm from the loop invariant before writing Java bounds updates.
questions.answer: Maintain that any possible matching index lies in the current inclusive [lo,hi]. Equality returns; comparison proves one half cannot match, so set lo=mid+1 or hi=mid-1. The interval shrinks until empty, proving termination and absence.

questions.question: If the sorted input is empty, which condition prevents reading its midpoint?
questions.answer: Initialize hi=n-1 and enter only while lo<=hi. For n=0, hi=-1 so no midpoint is read. A half-open variant instead uses while(lo<hi) and also performs no read for [0,0).

questions.question: How would a binary search over a monotone predicate differ from direct equality search?
questions.answer: Search for the boundary where a monotone predicate changes false to true, returning an insertion point even without exact equality. State which side is known true/false and preserve half-open bounds; feasibility must actually be monotone.

days.focus: Answer three mixed prompts in 15 minutes; spend 35 minutes repairing one failed code/design element and 5 logging evidence.

questions.question: How would you refactor a payment switch statement into strategies while keeping validation order observable?
questions.answer: Keep common validation and idempotency outside the strategy dispatch, then select a strategy by payment type through an explicit registry. Preserve ordered validation/error behavior with contract tests; extracting classes should not silently change which failure or side effect occurs first.

questions.question: Show an exception-to-HTTP mapping that avoids leaking account data in error responses.
questions.answer: Use a centralized exception handler returning a stable code, safe message and correlation ID. Map validation/conflict/not-found/authentication appropriately, log restricted diagnostic context separately and avoid revealing whether another tenant's account exists; the accompanying sketch shows the response boundary.

questions.question: How would you inject Clock and a bank client so retries can be tested without sleeping?
questions.answer: Inject Clock for timestamps, a monotonic/fake elapsed-time source for deadlines and a bank-client interface returning controlled outcomes. Inject the scheduler/sleeper too, so tests advance virtual time and simulate retryable, permanent and unknown responses without real sleeps.

questions.question: Sketch a Java value object for currency and amount that forbids adding different currencies.
questions.answer: Use an immutable Money value containing Currency and normalized BigDecimal with explicit scale/rounding. Its add method checks matching currencies before arithmetic; reject implicit conversion and preserve an explicit FX operation with rate/audit evidence.

questions.question: Write SQL identifying duplicate settlement references while retaining the individual offending row IDs.
questions.answer: Use COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY provider_id,settlement_ref) in a subquery, then filter count>1 while retaining each row ID. Include all fields defining true uniqueness; GROUP BY alone loses the individual offending rows.

questions.question: Design a repository method whose update count proves an expected account version was consumed.
questions.answer: Return the affected-row count from UPDATE ... SET version=version+1,... WHERE id=:id AND version=:expected. One means the expected version was consumed; zero means stale/missing or failed business predicates, which may need a separate authorized distinction.

questions.question: How would you return a stable public payment state while internal recovery steps are still running?
questions.answer: Map internal retry/reconciliation substates to a truthful stable public PENDING/UNKNOWN until authoritative evidence confirms a final result. Keep operation ID and observation metadata stable and provide status lookup; do not leak implementation phases as falsely final business outcomes.

questions.question: Sketch an event envelope containing identity, aggregate version and schema version; what does each field protect?
questions.answer: Include eventId for logical dedupe, aggregateId/version for per-entity ordering/concurrency, schemaVersion for payload interpretation, and occurredAt/producer metadata for diagnosis. These fields solve different problems; a timestamp cannot replace an aggregate sequence or stable identity.

questions.question: How would you combine multiple dependency failures into a response without treating an empty result as success?
questions.answer: Collect typed success/failure/unknown outcomes per dependency under one deadline and derive the response from the business policy. Preserve diagnostic causes and required-dependency failures; an empty collection is not proof of successful zero results unless that is the explicit contract.

questions.question: Design a replay command that requires an explicit date range and records every attempted event ID.
questions.answer: Require explicit bounded date range, source/version and tenant scope, with dry-run/approval controls as appropriate. Persist run identity and every attempted event/result, preserve original business IDs and rate-limit execution; retries must remain auditable and idempotent.

questions.question: Write a controller test that verifies a repeated idempotency key with a changed amount is rejected.
questions.answer: Send the same tenant/key with amount100 then amount101. Assert a conflict response and exactly one durable payment/provider effect with the original fingerprint, using the real service/idempotency boundary where possible; a controller-only mock proves mapping, not database arbitration.

questions.question: How would you make cache invalidation retryable after a committed database update?
questions.answer: Persist a versioned invalidation/outbox intent in the same transaction as the update, then retry its delivery idempotently. Prefer cache writes that cannot overwrite newer versions; cache correctness must survive relay duplicates and temporary cache unavailability.

questions.question: Sketch executor metrics that distinguish rejection, queue wait, execution time and cancellation.
questions.answer: Instrument accepted/rejected submissions, enqueue-to-start duration, task execution duration and cancellation request/completion separately. Tag by bounded pool/task class, not request ID; distinguish a cancelled handle from a task or transport that actually stopped.

questions.question: What contract makes an LLD diagram implementable: method signatures, state transitions, invariants or all three? Demonstrate on one wallet operation.
questions.answer: All three are needed. For debit(operationId,amount,expectedVersion), define allowed positive same-currency input, insufficient-funds/conflict outcomes, atomic balance+journal transition, idempotent replay and concurrency/version rules. Signatures alone cannot establish the wallet's financial behavior.

questions.question: A wallet LLD supports balance updates but no audit journal. Add the smallest durable model that permits reconciliation without rewriting history.
questions.answer: Add an immutable journal header keyed by operation identity and balanced debit/credit lines with account, amount, currency and timestamps. Commit journal and balance projection atomically with constraints/idempotency. Correct errors using linked reversals/adjustments, and reconcile projections against the journal rather than editing history to match a desired balance.

questions.question: A partial batch retries every item after one failure and duplicates successful notifications. Which checkpoint and per-item identity would you add?
questions.answer: Persist per-item delivery identity, status and provider evidence, and checkpoint only completed work under a replay-safe batch identity. Retry failed/unknown items according to their external outcome policy, not the whole batch indiscriminately. Track partial completion and verify that already-delivered email/SMS jobs are not resent after a crash.

questions.question: A rate limiter passes sequential tests but fails under simultaneous boundary refills. Design a deterministic test and an atomic implementation boundary.
questions.answer: With a fake clock at one refill boundary, gate multiple workers before consume and release them together, collecting every result with bounded waits. Assert grants do not exceed the one refilled allowance. Make elapsed-time refill and token decrement one synchronized/CAS/store-script transition; independent atomic fields are insufficient.

questions.question: Why should tests not demand one exact chosen-index list when multiple maximum-value selections exist?
questions.answer: Several nonadjacent subsets can have the same optimal sum. Verify returned indices are valid/nonadjacent and their sum equals an independent optimum, rather than rejecting another valid tie choice unless deterministic tie-breaking is specified.

questions.question: If the input must be processed from an iterator, can the rolling-state algorithm still work?
questions.answer: Yes. Process values in order with the previous two prefix optima, using constant auxiliary state. You can return the best value without random access; reconstructing chosen indices requires additional retained information or another pass.

questions.question: What extra requirement arises if the method must support updates to old house values between queries?
questions.answer: Rolling DP assumes a fixed left-to-right input. Updating old values changes later prefix optima, so repeated recomputation is O(n) per update; faster dynamic queries need additional composable state, such as a carefully designed segment tree.

questions.question: During a re-solve, prove that every valid solution either excludes the last house or includes it with its neighbor excluded.
questions.answer: Partition valid solutions into those skipping the last house, bounded by the previous-prefix optimum, and those taking it, which must skip its neighbor and add the two-back optimum. These exhaustive disjoint choices yield the recurrence.

questions.question: How does a per-selected-house fee alter the value used in a take transition?
questions.answer: Subtract the fee from each house's value in the take transition. If selecting none is allowed, keep the empty optimum zero, so negative net choices are skipped; a mandatory-selection variant needs a different base/state contract.

questions.question: Why does recomputing both recursive branches without memoization repeat the same prefix subproblems?
questions.answer: Both branches eventually request the optimum for many identical earlier prefixes, causing exponential recomputation. Memoization computes each prefix once; rolling DP evaluates the same dependency graph in increasing order with only needed prior states.

days.focus: Run a 25-minute oral mini-mock and a 25-minute correction; record R and A independently in the final 5 minutes.

questions.question: In a 25-minute payment design mock, which one end-to-end failure path would you trace after drawing the write path?
questions.answer: Trace bank success followed by lost response/process crash before local confirmation, then client retry and callback/reconciliation. Explain persisted operation identity, unknown state, ledger effect and idempotency at each boundary; this exposes more correctness assumptions than a happy-path component list.

questions.question: How would a Java mock distinguish a visibility fix from a mutual-exclusion fix using one runnable example?
questions.answer: Use a volatile stop flag to demonstrate visibility of a control change, then show volatile int counter++ still loses updates under a forced read/read/write/write schedule. Use a lock or atomic increment for mutual exclusion/atomicity; visibility alone does not protect compound actions.

questions.question: Given a low-selectivity status predicate and a narrow time range, how would you defend a composite index order using the plan?
questions.answer: Compare candidate plans using actual rows scanned, filtering, sort and I/O for representative status/time distributions. Equality-before-range can help, but low selectivity, covering/order needs and engine behavior matter; defend the measured workload choice rather than one memorized rule.

questions.question: After adding an index, which plan and write-load measurements might show that a faster read harmed the system overall?
questions.answer: Measure read latency/rows/I/O alongside posting throughput, write amplification, lock waits, buffer pressure, storage and maintenance cost. A removed read sort can coexist with worse business throughput, so judge the mixed workload and SLOs.

questions.question: When a retryable update changes its generated request ID on every attempt, which idempotency guarantee is broken?
questions.answer: Physical retries no longer share one logical operation identity, so durable dedupe/provider idempotency sees each as a new request. Preserve the original business key across attempts and use separate attempt IDs only for tracing.

questions.question: How would you defend synchronous confirmation versus asynchronous acceptance for a bank operation with a long tail?
questions.answer: Synchronous confirmation gives immediate finality only within the provider latency/reliability budget. Durable asynchronous acceptance lowers coupling and exposes pending/status/reconciliation semantics. Choose according to the user requirement and deadline rather than promising immediate confirmation despite an unbounded bank tail.

questions.question: Which invariant makes a compensating credit safe if the original debit may still be pending externally?
questions.answer: Do not issue a definitive compensating credit unless the original financial state and compensation authority are established. If debit outcome is unknown, reconcile first or use an explicitly modeled provisional accounting process; compensation must be uniquely identified, balanced and state-validated.

questions.question: How should a Kafka consumer preserve aggregate ordering while retrying one poisoned event?
questions.answer: Pause/block that aggregate or partition until the poison event is repaired, or use a sequenced retry workflow that buffers later versions. Sending it to a DLQ and processing successors can violate order; define when skipping is business-safe and auditable.

questions.question: If rate-limiter storage fails, what business criteria decide fail-open versus fail-closed behavior?
questions.answer: Fail closed when the limiter protects financial correctness, abuse or a hard contractual quota; fail open with bounded local protection for selected availability-oriented traffic if the business accepts the risk. Specify outage duration, fallback limits and reconciliation rather than one universal policy.

questions.question: How would you compare pessimistic locking, optimistic retries and an atomic SQL update for a hot wallet?
questions.answer: Pessimistic locks serialize with wait/deadlock cost; optimistic retries work best with lower conflicts and can amplify a hot key; atomic conditional SQL often suits a simple balance predicate. Compare measured contention and invariants, including the journal transaction and retry safety.

questions.question: When a mock interviewer halves memory limits, how would you revise a heap-heavy design without claiming unchanged capacity?
questions.answer: Reduce retained state, concurrency and cache weights, consider streaming/spill and preserve native-memory headroom. Re-run capacity tests and state revised throughput/latency limits; halving memory need not preserve the original capacity or algorithm choice.

questions.question: How would you distinguish source ownership from team contribution in a project architecture explanation?
questions.answer: Explain the team's architecture and then name the specific proposals, modules, migrations or operational decisions you implemented/led. Support the scope with artifacts and distinguish influence/review from sole ownership.

questions.question: What evidence would you request before accepting that a Java 25 feature caused a production regression?
questions.answer: Request exact JDK/build/options, workload, old/new controlled runs, profiler/JFR evidence and a minimal reproducer. Check library compatibility and configuration changes too; temporal coincidence with Java25 does not establish a language feature as the cause.

questions.question: How would you demonstrate a recovery process works when the backup has never been restored in a test?
questions.answer: Run an isolated restore exercise including data, schema/version, configuration, keys and dependent services, then validate invariants and measure RPO/RTO. Until that succeeds, describe recovery as unverified rather than demonstrating confidence with a diagram.

questions.question: Your HLD relies on a single Redis primary for money correctness. Describe a failover timeline and choose a durable authority.
questions.answer: Show primary acknowledgment followed by failure before replica persistence, then a retry accepted on a replica lacking the key. Use a durable transactional ledger/operation registry as authority with the required replication guarantee, and treat Redis as cache/coordination optimization. Explicitly define the failure scope in which an acknowledged money effect survives.

questions.question: A local lock prevents duplicate charges on one pod while six pods are deployed. Where must the shared concurrency decision move?
questions.answer: Move arbitration to shared durable storage using tenant-scoped uniqueness and atomic operation/effect state, with provider idempotency for external calls. One JVM lock coordinates only that process. Test simultaneous requests across multiple instances and crash/replay behavior; a shared cache lock alone is not a durable financial record.

questions.question: A query optimization removes a sort but returns inconsistent pagination under ties. Defend a complete ordering and cursor design.
questions.answer: Order by a stable complete tuple, such as non-null created_at plus unique ID, and encode both in the cursor with matching lexicographic predicates. Specify null and concurrent-update semantics and preserve the required sort/index order. Removing a sort is not an optimization if it changes the pagination contract.

questions.question: Why can testing only the total intersection size miss an incorrect selected value?
questions.answer: Two outputs can have equal size but contain different values. Assert each result belongs to both inputs, no result duplicates exist, and every value common to both is present; compare sets with an independent reference.

questions.question: Construct tests where inputs share no values, all values, and only their last values.
questions.answer: No overlap: [1,2]/[3,4] ->[]; full overlap: [1,2]/[2,1] ->{1,2}; last-only: [1,7]/[2,7] ->{7}. Include duplicate runs to verify distinct output.

questions.question: If the two inputs are already sorted, how does that change the preferred algorithm?
questions.answer: Use two pointers with O(n+m) scan time and O(1) auxiliary state excluding output, skipping duplicate matches. No sorting or membership set is necessary because the sorted-order precondition already holds.

questions.question: What input-mutation decision must be documented before sorting either array?
questions.answer: Document whether inputs may be reordered. If mutation is forbidden, clone before sorting and include copy space; choose hashing if preserving order and the memory trade-off make it preferable.

questions.question: How would you property-test that intersection(A,B) equals intersection(B,A) as a set?
questions.answer: Generate random array pairs and compare result sets for intersection(A,B) and intersection(B,A), ignoring permitted output order. Also compare with a separately built reference set to avoid two symmetric implementations sharing the same bug.

questions.question: During an unseen Easy mock, explain the distinct-output requirement before choosing your data structure.
questions.answer: State that each common value appears once regardless of input multiplicity and that output order is unspecified unless requested. Then choose a membership set with removal-on-match or a separate result set; this avoids accidentally solving multiset intersection.

questions.question: Your cumulative lab loses an acknowledged message during a crash; where would you place durable acknowledgement?
questions.answer: Acknowledge only after the message intent/effect is durably recorded at the promised boundary. For a consumer, commit offsets after durable idempotent business completion; for API acceptance, persist the operation/outbox before success. Define exactly which failures the storage acknowledgment survives.

questions.question: Two corrected tests still share a static fixture; how could their execution order hide the original defect?
questions.answer: One test may initialize or clean state the other silently relies on, so the corrected test passes only in that order. Use isolated fixtures, reset static state or remove it, and run reversed/randomized/parallel order to expose the dependency.

questions.question: An executor cancellation marks a Future done while work continues; which cooperative-stop check belongs in the task?
questions.answer: Check interruption/stop state at bounded intervals and use interruptible operations or explicit client cancellation/deadlines. Propagate/reassert interrupts appropriately and exit; work that ignores cancellation can continue after Future.isDone reports true.

questions.question: How would you prove the repaired outbox relay tolerates termination between publish and acknowledgement?
questions.answer: Kill or fault the relay after broker acknowledgment but before database completion marking, restart it and observe republish with the same event ID. Assert the consumer applies the business effect once and the outbox eventually completes, with bounded test waits and captured evidence.

questions.question: Your memory fix replaces an unbounded cache with an entry cap; what value-size distribution could still exceed the memory budget?
questions.answer: A few large or growing values can exceed memory even under a fixed entry count. Test heavy-tailed sizes and retained object graphs, use weight-based admission/eviction and immutable/reweighed values, and include keys and overhead in the practical budget.

questions.question: A bank reconciliation repair finds both a timeout and a later success callback; how must state transitions arbitrate them?
questions.answer: Client timeout leaves the financial result unknown, while authenticated success is authoritative evidence. Use versioned conditional transitions and stable operation identity so success applies once and stale timeout/retry handlers cannot overwrite it as failed.

questions.question: After fixing a lock order, what multi-operation path could reacquire locks in the opposite order?
questions.answer: Audit callbacks, logging hooks, cleanup, nested operations and error paths that acquire additional locks. A corrected main path can still deadlock through a reverse-order callback; enforce one documented order or invoke external code outside the protected locks.

questions.question: How would a production-like data skew test validate the corrected SQL plan?
questions.answer: Generate representative hot/cold keys, correlated predicates, cardinality and bind distributions at realistic scale. Compare estimated/actual plan rows, spill/I/O and tail latency; uniform tiny fixtures cannot establish that the skew-related regression is fixed.

questions.question: A rollback test passes without flushing the entity; what database constraint error could still be invisible?
questions.answer: Deferred inserts/updates or transaction-end checks may never reach the database before the test rolls back. Flush and, where needed, commit to expose unique, foreign-key, not-null or deferred constraint violations, then verify through fresh state.

questions.question: Before merging the lab fixes, which evidence links each changed line to its original failure reproduction?
questions.answer: Keep the failing reproducer, root-cause evidence, minimal patch and passing regression result linked per defect. Review unrelated changes separately and include integration/chaos evidence where the failure crossed process or commit boundaries; line coverage alone does not demonstrate causal repair.

questions.question: After repairing two lab defects, a chaos test kills the consumer during offset commit. Which invariant and observable result determine whether the lab is finished?
questions.answer: The invariant is that every acknowledged/committed record has its durable effect and replay never duplicates it; unfinished work remains recoverable. Kill around commit, restart and compare event IDs, dedupe/effect rows and offsets. Completion requires eventual backlog recovery and correct balances, not merely a process that restarts or lag that reaches zero.

questions.question: A manual financial correction fixes balances but bypasses the journal. How would you repair the repair while preserving an audit trail?
questions.answer: Preserve the manual action evidence and reconstruct the authoritative missing financial event. Add approved linked adjustment/reversal journal entries under a controlled operation identity, then reconcile the balance projection and totals without disguising or deleting the original bypass. Require independent review and audit metadata according to the financial process.

questions.question: A CI test is flaky only with parallel execution. How would you isolate shared state, timing assumptions and environment limits?
questions.answer: Run the smallest conflicting test pair with phase gates and per-test resources, then inspect static fixtures, shared database rows, ports, clocks and executor limits. Capture worker failures and bounded waits; distinguish actual data races from environment starvation. Remove shared assumptions rather than adding arbitrary sleeps or retries.

questions.question: How could an accidental eight-direction neighbor array alter a payment-region grouping algorithm built from this code?
questions.answer: Eight-direction traversal merges diagonal land regions that four-direction connectivity keeps separate. For [[1,0],[0,1]], the correct four-connected count is two, while eight-direction code returns one; state the adjacency contract before reuse.

questions.question: What checks distinguish string '1' data from character '1' cells in the Java grid model?
questions.answer: Use char[][] with literals '1'/'0', not numeric 1/0 or String comparisons. Validate parsing separately if input starts as List<String>; test one land cell, one water cell and malformed symbols under the documented contract.

questions.question: During a timed re-solve, explain the distinction between total cell visits and number of component launches.
questions.answer: The outer scan examines every cell once, and each land cell is marked/processed at most once, giving O(rows*cols) work. A component launch occurs only at previously unvisited land, so its count is the island answer, not total land-cell visits.

questions.question: If you return island bounding boxes as well as counts, which state must reset for every newly discovered component?
questions.answer: Reset minRow,maxRow,minCol,maxCol for the starting cell of each new component, update them during traversal and emit one box afterward. Do not carry extrema from the previous island; test separated components in opposite corners.

When an incident hypothesis is plausible but unverified, how would you state it while naming the next discriminating measurement?
A previously safe retry becomes unsafe after a provider API change; what compatibility contract should alert the team?
How can a backend service remain available while refusing operations whose financial correctness cannot be established?
Which Java version and database assumptions would you state before defending your transaction and concurrency answer?
What should a project deep dive contain when the original performance baseline is no longer available?
How would you turn one unresolved race into a bounded reproduction and an explicit open engineering risk?
senior: A settlement file is delivered twice six weeks apart, after the short-lived cache expires. Which durable identity and retention policy prevent a second posting?
A bank debit succeeds while your local database is unavailable, then a callback arrives twice. Explain the recovery state machine and operator evidence.
